stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss of 4 kg, and increasing dyspnoea on exertion. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 2 years ago for calcific aortic stenosis and is otherwise well. He denies any recent dental procedure but had a dental cleaning 6 weeks ago and did not receive antibiotic prophylaxis.

On examination he has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a small linear haemorrhage under his right great toenail. Splinter haemorrhages are visible on his left index finger. Three sets of blood cultures drawn 12 hours apart have all grown Streptococcus sanguinis, sensitive to benzylpenicillin. A transoesophageal echocardiogram today demonstrates a 6 mm mobile echogenic mass on the aortic side of the prosthetic aortic valve with new mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 110/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-180), white cell count 14 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), CRP 82 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Blood cultures: three sets over 24 hours all positive for Streptococcus sanguinis
data_table.Echocardiography: 6 mm mobile mass on aortic side of prosthetic aortic valve, new mild aortic regurgitation

lead_in: Which of the following statements correctly categorises the modified Duke criteria met by this presentation?

options.text: This meets 1 major and 2 minor criteria only, which is insufficient for a definite diagnosis and requires a possible endocarditis classification while further criteria are sought
options.rationale: The echocardiographic vegetation with new regurgitation on a prosthetic valve is a separate MAJOR criterion, not a minor. Two majors are present. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets 1 major and 4 minor criteria, which meets a definite endocarditis classification and requires no additional echocardiographic imaging at all
options.rationale: There are not 4 minor criteria here (fever above 38 is one minor, splinter haemorrhages are one minor); more importantly the echocardiographic evidence is major and completes a 2-major definite diagnosis. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets 5 minor criteria and no major criteria, allowing a definite endocarditis diagnosis to be made once further blood culture sets are drawn to confirm
options.rationale: Persistent bacteraemia with typical organism and echocardiographic vegetation are both majors, not minors. This case is diagnosed on 2 majors. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets neither major nor sufficient minor criteria and requires cardiac magnetic resonance imaging today before a definite classification can be applied
options.rationale: Two majors are clearly present. Cardiac MRI is an adjunct in problem cases but is not required to make the diagnosis here. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets 2 major criteria (typical organism on persistently positive blood cultures plus echocardiographic vegetation with new regurgitation), sufficient for a definite endocarditis diagnosis
options.rationale: Modified Duke definite endocarditis requires either 2 majors, or 1 major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors. Here the typical organism from persistently positive blood cultures satisfies one major, and the echocardiographic vegetation plus new regurgitation satisfies the second. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria establish definite endocarditis with 2 majors, 1 major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors. Typical organism from persistently positive blood cultures is one major; echocardiographic vegetation with new valvular regurgitation is a second. This patient meets both, warranting a definite diagnosis and immediate treatment planning with cardiology and cardiac surgery input given the prosthetic valve.
key_points: Major criteria: typical organism in 2 or more separate blood cultures; echocardiographic evidence (vegetation, abscess, new prosthetic dehiscence, new regurgitation)
Minor criteria: predisposing condition, fever above 38, vascular phenomena (splinters, Janeway), immunologic (Osler, Roth), microbiological non-major
Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires early cardiac surgery review
explanation.pearls: The trap is calling splinter haemorrhages a major. They are a minor vascular phenomenon. Echocardiographic vegetation is the major.

sources.label: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

subtopic_detail: COPD GOLD Group E escalation therapy
stem:
A 68-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history and moderate COPD attends his general practice for review after a hospital admission for infective exacerbation 4 weeks ago requiring intravenous antibiotics. This is his second exacerbation this year, the first being managed in the community with oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Spirometry shows post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 55 percent predicted with a modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea score of 2 out of 4.

He stopped smoking during the last admission and has re-engaged with pulmonary rehabilitation. His current inhaled therapy is tiotropium 18 microgram once daily via HandiHaler alone. He reports good adherence and correct inhaler technique demonstrated at the pharmacy. His eosinophil count on the recent admission was 320 cells per microlitre (150-500) and he has no history of asthma or atopic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: post-bronchodilator FEV1 55 percent predicted, mMRC 2 out of 4, peripheral eosinophil count 320 cells per microlitre
data_table.Exacerbation history: one community-managed exacerbation and one hospitalisation in the past 12 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his inhaled therapy?

options.text: Switch tiotropium to a fixed dose LABA plus LAMA (long-acting beta-agonist plus long-acting muscarinic antagonist) combination inhaler in a single device
options.rationale: For GOLD Group E COPD (2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalisation in the past year), GOLD 2023 recommends escalating from LAMA monotherapy to LABA plus LAMA. Triple therapy (LABA plus LAMA plus ICS) is added if exacerbations persist AND eosinophils are at or above 300. His eosinophil count is 320 but the initial escalation is dual bronchodilator. (Source: GOLD 2023 COPD Report; Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Continue tiotropium monotherapy and add a short-acting beta-agonist reliever only, with review in 3 months and repeat spirometry at that time
options.rationale: Group E COPD requires escalation of maintenance therapy, not continuation of monotherapy. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Switch immediately to triple therapy (LABA plus LAMA plus inhaled corticosteroid) as a single combination inhaler on the basis of the elevated eosinophil count
options.rationale: Triple therapy is indicated for Group E patients with continued exacerbations on LABA plus LAMA and eosinophils at or above 300. Jumping straight to triple therapy skips the intermediate step. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Add oral theophylline modified release 200 mg twice daily for its anti-inflammatory effect and repeat serum drug levels at 2 weeks after initiation
options.rationale: Theophylline is a last-resort option due to its narrow therapeutic index and drug interactions and is not recommended before dual bronchodilator escalation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Commence long term oral prednisolone 5 mg daily to reduce the risk of further exacerbations over the next 12 months of maintenance treatment
options.rationale: Chronic oral corticosteroid therapy is not recommended for stable COPD outside end-stage disease due to systemic toxicity without exacerbation benefit. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

explanation.summary: GOLD Group E (2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalisation in the past year) requires escalation from LAMA monotherapy to LABA plus LAMA. Triple therapy is reserved for patients with continued exacerbations on dual bronchodilator AND eosinophils at or above 300. Non-pharmacological measures (pulmonary rehab, smoking cessation, vaccination) run in parallel.
key_points: Group E: 2 or more moderate exacerbations OR 1 hospitalisation in the past year
Escalate LAMA to LABA plus LAMA first; add ICS only if continued exacerbations and eosinophils at or above 300
COPD-X aligns with GOLD 2023 in Australia
explanation.pearls: Do not skip to triple therapy in a patient with only one prior hospitalisation. Dual bronchodilator is the correct next step; add ICS only if that fails and eosinophils support it.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

stem:
A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a fall onto her head at home. She has an obvious right-sided haematoma over the temporal region and has vomited twice. On arrival her GCS is 13 (E3V4M6) and she is confused about time and place. A non-contrast CT scan of the brain shows a 15 mm right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 6 mm midline shift.

She has atrial fibrillation and takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VA score 5). Her last dose was this morning approximately 4 hours ago. Her renal function is normal with creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90) and her weight is 68 kg. She has no other bleeding sources and no ongoing extracranial haemorrhage. Neurosurgical consultation has been sought and they advise urgent reversal is required.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 148/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, GCS 13
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2), activated partial thromboplastin time 32 seconds (25-35)
data_table.Imaging: non-contrast CT brain with 15 mm right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage and 6 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal agent?

options.text: Administer intravenous idarucizumab 5 g in two 2.5 g intravenous bolus doses within 15 minutes of each other for urgent DOAC reversal now
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is specific for the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran, not the factor Xa inhibitor apixaban. It has no effect on apixaban. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.text: Administer intravenous andexanet alfa in a bolus and infusion regimen dosed per the last dose and time since ingestion of apixaban
options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is a specific reversal agent for the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban and is approved in Australia for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding. Dosing is stratified by last dose amount and time since last dose. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.text: Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 25 units/kg for warfarin-type coagulopathy reversal
options.rationale: This is the AU reversal protocol for warfarin-associated bleeding, not apixaban. Vitamin K has no role in reversing DOACs. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.text: Administer intravenous fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg as the first-line reversal for apixaban-associated intracerebral haemorrhage in this patient
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma does not effectively reverse DOAC anticoagulant effect and is not recommended as first-line. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

options.text: Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g bolus as monotherapy for apixaban reversal in this haemorrhagic stroke without other reversal agents
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid does not reverse the DOAC anticoagulant effect. It has an emerging adjunct role but is not a specific DOAC reversal agent. (Source: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus)
source_refs: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

explanation.summary: Reversal agents for direct oral anticoagulants are drug-specific. Andexanet alfa reverses the factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban; idarucizumab reverses the direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran. Where andexanet alfa is unavailable, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate at 50 units/kg is used off-label. Vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma are ineffective for DOAC reversal.
key_points: Andexanet alfa for apixaban and rivaroxaban; idarucizumab for dabigatran
4-factor PCC at 50 units/kg is off-label alternative for factor Xa inhibitor reversal
Vitamin K, FFP, TXA are not effective DOAC reversal agents
explanation.pearls: Match the reversal to the DOAC mechanism. Confusing idarucizumab and andexanet is the classic exam trap.

sources.label: HSANZ Warfarin and DOAC Reversal Consensus

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of loin pain, dysuria and fever. On arrival she is confused, cool peripherally, and has a mottled abdomen. Her past history includes type 2 diabetes on metformin and long-standing recurrent urinary tract infection. She has no known drug allergies.

On examination she has significant right renal angle tenderness and a distended bladder. Her point-of-care ultrasound shows moderate right hydronephrosis with debris in the collecting system. A urinary catheter has been placed with 300 mL of purulent urine drained on insertion. The Australian Sepsis Network hour-1 bundle has been activated. Urology have been contacted regarding potential percutaneous nephrostomy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), white cell count 18 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), venous lactate 4.8 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90), CRP 240 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Bedside investigations: catheter urine dip 4+ leukocytes, nitrites positive, moderate blood; blood glucose 12.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the correct order of the hour-1 bundle interventions?

options.text: Commence vasopressors first for hypotension, then administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, then measure lactate, then obtain cultures, then commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation over 3 hours in a controlled ICU setting
options.rationale: Vasopressors are added only after fluid resuscitation has failed to restore MAP to 65 or above. Starting them first violates the bundle. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Administer antibiotics first without cultures, then measure lactate, then commence crystalloid resuscitation at 20 mL/kg to reduce risk of pulmonary oedema, then obtain blood and urine cultures
options.rationale: Cultures should be obtained BEFORE antibiotics whenever possible without delaying antibiotics. Fluid dose is 30 mL/kg, not 20. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Await urinary culture results before administering antibiotics to guide narrow-spectrum therapy, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid, measure lactate, and consider vasopressors once organism identified in the microbiology laboratory
options.rationale: Antibiotics must be given within 1 hour empirically for septic shock. Waiting for cultures increases mortality. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Measure lactate, obtain blood and urine cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics (empirical piperacillin-tazobactam and gentamicin), commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation, and start vasopressors for persistent hypotension after fluid
options.rationale: The Surviving Sepsis and Australian Sepsis Network hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate, obtain cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and start vasopressors if MAP under 65 despite fluid. Urgent source control (nephrostomy) is added in obstructed pyelonephritis. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

options.text: Perform urgent contrast CT abdomen and pelvis to identify the source, then obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid, and measure lactate after resuscitation is completed
options.rationale: Imaging should not delay the bundle. The source is already identified on point-of-care ultrasound with confirmed obstruction and pyuria. (Source: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway)
source_refs: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway

explanation.summary: The Australian Sepsis Network hour-1 bundle is a fixed sequence: measure lactate, obtain cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics, commence 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, and start vasopressors if MAP under 65 despite fluid. Source control (in this case percutaneous nephrostomy for the obstructed infected kidney) is added urgently but does not delay the bundle.
key_points: Cultures before antibiotics unless drawing cultures would delay antibiotics
30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate greater than 4
Vasopressor of choice is noradrenaline; target MAP at least 65 mmHg
Source control in obstructed pyelonephritis is percutaneous nephrostomy urgently
explanation.pearls: Empiric AU cover for community urosepsis is piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (or ceftriaxone plus gentamicin). Adjust with cultures at 24 to 48 hours.

sources.label: Australian Sepsis Network Adult Sepsis Pathway
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Sepsis and septic shock

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in known Addison's during acute illness
stem:
A 42-year-old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is brought to a rural emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting from gastroenteritis. She takes hydrocortisone 15 mg on waking and 5 mg at 4 p.m., and fludrocortisone 100 microgram in the morning. She reports she doubled her hydrocortisone dose orally 12 hours ago but has vomited each subsequent dose within 30 minutes of taking it.

She is drowsy and confused. Her family confirms she has been unable to keep down fluids. There is no fever and no localising infective source apart from the gastroenteritis. She wears a medical alert bracelet identifying her as having primary adrenal insufficiency. Her partner has brought her intramuscular hydrocortisone emergency kit from home.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 74/44, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.30
data_table.Bedside investigations: 12-lead ECG with sinus tachycardia and peaked T waves in the precordial leads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg immediately in place of hydrocortisone and await the results of a short synacthen test performed later today at bedside
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is used only when the diagnosis of primary adrenal insufficiency is not yet made and a synacthen test is planned in the next few hours. Diagnosis is already established; hydrocortisone is the correct choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL for hyperkalaemia and defer steroid dosing until potassium is under 5.0 mmol/L on repeat testing
options.rationale: The hyperkalaemia will correct with steroid, fluid and glucose (via insulin) therapy. Deferring hydrocortisone is dangerous and inappropriate; calcium can be given for ECG changes but does not replace hydrocortisone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Administer oral prednisolone 25 mg with an antiemetic and observe for 4 hours before deciding on intravenous replacement therapy in the resuscitation area
options.rationale: Oral steroid in a vomiting patient is unreliable and delays effective replacement. Parenteral hydrocortisone is required immediately. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Administer intravenous fludrocortisone 200 microgram immediately as mineralocorticoid replacement therapy for the electrolyte disturbance in adrenal crisis
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is oral only and its mineralocorticoid effect is provided by high-dose hydrocortisone (which has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity at 100 mg doses). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal insufficiency)

options.text: Administer intramuscular or intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours, with concurrent saline and dextrose resuscitation
options.rationale: Suspected or confirmed adrenal crisis requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg over 24 hours, plus fluid and glucose resuscitation. Delay for confirmatory testing is inappropriate. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in a known Addison's patient with vomiting and hypotension requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours). Concurrent 0.9 percent sodium chloride and dextrose correct volume, glucose, and electrolyte disturbances. Fludrocortisone is not needed acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV stat, then 200 mg over 24 hours or 50 mg every 6 hours
0.9 percent saline resuscitation and 5 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia and volume
Sick day rules: double or triple oral dose for illness; parenteral if vomiting; carry emergency kit
explanation.pearls: The single commonest cause of death in Addison's is failure to give parenteral hydrocortisone during acute illness. Never wait for confirmatory tests when the diagnosis is known.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia Adrenal Insufficiency Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Hyponatraemia correction rate ceiling to avoid osmotic demyelination
stem:
A 78-year-old woman is admitted from a residential aged care facility with 5 days of increasing confusion after a viral gastroenteritis and 4 days of poor oral intake. She takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for hypertension and citalopram 20 mg daily for depression. On admission her serum sodium is 112 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L, urea 4.8 mmol/L (3-8), and urine sodium 42 mmol/L (spot).

She is drowsy but rousable, has no seizures, and has a GCS of 12 (E3V4M5). Serum osmolality is 240 mOsm/kg (275-295) and urine osmolality is 380 mOsm/kg. She has no oedema and has an estimated 1 to 2 percent volume depletion on clinical assessment. She has no known alcohol use disorder and no history of chronic kidney disease. Family confirm the confusion has been progressive over the past 3 days.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees, GCS 12
data_table.Investigations: sodium 112 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 4.8 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), serum osmolality 240 mOsm/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 380 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 42 mmol/L

lead_in: Given her symptoms, what is the most appropriate rate ceiling for correction of her serum sodium over the first 24 hours?

options.text: Correction should not exceed 8 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (with 6 mmol/L preferred in high-risk patients), after an initial 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus for symptomatic hyponatraemia
options.rationale: AU/international consensus recommends a maximum sodium rise of 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (some experts prefer 6 in high-risk groups: elderly, hypokalaemia, chronic hyponatraemia, malnutrition). Given severe symptoms, initial 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus is given, then repeat until symptoms improve, targeting an initial 4 to 6 mmol/L rise in the first few hours, but the 24-hour ceiling remains 8. (Source: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia Guideline; ANZ Renal Society)

options.text: Correction may safely proceed at 15 mmol/L in the first 24 hours if the patient has severe neurological symptoms, using continuous 3 percent hypertonic saline infusion
options.rationale: Rapid correction exceeding 10 to 12 mmol/L per 24 hours substantially raises the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome. This is unsafe. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)

options.text: Correction should aim for a return to normal sodium (135 mmol/L) within 12 hours of admission, as the confusion and drowsiness indicate impending herniation and immediate normalisation is life-saving
options.rationale: Attempting to normalise sodium quickly is a classical error and directly causes osmotic demyelination. Immediate life-threatening features are addressed with a small bolus, not full normalisation. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)

options.text: Correction should be limited to 4 mmol/L in the first 24 hours because the patient is asymptomatic and there is no urgency to correct the sodium in this setting
options.rationale: She is not asymptomatic (drowsy, GCS 12) and 4 mmol/L is too conservative for a symptomatic presentation. The correct ceiling is 8 mmol/L. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)

options.text: Correction should proceed at 12 mmol/L in the first 24 hours because the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome only becomes significant beyond that rate of correction in a healthy adult
options.rationale: The safety threshold is 10 mmol/L per 24 hours; most guidelines set a lower operating ceiling of 8 mmol/L to leave margin for error. 12 exceeds the safe range. (Source: ANZ Renal Society Hyponatraemia Consensus)

explanation.summary: In chronic or subacute symptomatic hyponatraemia, the correction rate ceiling is 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (6 in high-risk groups). Severe symptoms (seizures, coma) are treated with a 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus, repeated as needed until symptoms improve, targeting an initial 4 to 6 mmol/L rise. Overcorrection is treated with 5 percent dextrose infusion and desmopressin if the rate exceeds the ceiling.
key_points: Maximum sodium rise in 24 hours: 8 mmol/L (6 in elderly, hypokalaemic, chronic, malnourished)
Severe symptoms: 100 mL 3 percent saline bolus, may repeat every 10 min for symptomatic control
Overcorrection re-lowered with 5 percent dextrose and desmopressin
explanation.pearls: Osmotic demyelination classically manifests 2 to 6 days after overcorrection with pseudobulbar palsy, quadriparesis and locked-in state. Once occurred it is largely irreversible.

sources.label: Spasovski et al. European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia Guideline. Eur J Endocrinol 2014

subtopic_detail: Type A aortic dissection with hypertension and stroke
stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department with sudden onset tearing central chest pain radiating to the back that began 90 minutes ago while shovelling in his garden. He has hypertension treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily and hyperlipidaemia treated with atorvastatin 40 mg nightly. He is now hemodynamically stable but continues to describe severe pain.

On arrival his right arm blood pressure is 176/98 and his left arm blood pressure is 128/72. His radial pulses are asymmetric. Neurological examination reveals right-sided hemiparesis (arm and leg 3 out of 5) and expressive dysphasia that began after arrival. A CT aortogram completed 15 minutes ago demonstrates a Stanford Type A dissection extending from the aortic root through the arch and involving the innominate artery, with a moderate pericardial effusion but no cardiac tamponade. Cardiothoracic surgery has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 176/98 right arm and 128/72 left arm, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), troponin I 0.02 microgram/L (less than 0.03), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), ECG with sinus rhythm and no acute ischaemic changes
data_table.Imaging: CT aortogram with Stanford Type A dissection root through arch, innominate artery involved, moderate pericardial effusion without tamponade

lead_in: In addition to arranging emergency cardiothoracic transfer, what is the most appropriate initial medical management?

options.text: Commence intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg for the acute ischaemic stroke, aiming to complete infusion within 60 minutes of stroke onset to salvage the penumbra
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is contraindicated in aortic dissection because of the catastrophic haemorrhagic risk. The hemiparesis reflects innominate artery involvement, not thromboembolic stroke. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)

options.text: Administer intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to target heart rate under 60 with intravenous glyceryl trinitrate for target systolic under 120 in the higher-reading arm, and analgesia
options.rationale: Type A dissection medical management is impulse control: a rate-limiting beta blocker (esmolol or labetalol) FIRST to blunt shear stress, followed by a vasodilator to reduce blood pressure to a systolic under 120 mmHg (measured in the higher-reading arm). Reversing this order can cause reflex tachycardia and worsen dissection. (Source: ANZ Society for Vascular Surgery Aortic Dissection Statement; Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

options.text: Administer intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion alone without a rate-limiting beta blocker to rapidly reduce systolic blood pressure to under 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Vasodilator without a rate-limiting agent causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic wall shear stress, worsening dissection propagation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)

options.text: Administer subcutaneous enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for suspected pulmonary embolism prophylaxis pending completion of CT pulmonary angiogram results
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because of haemorrhage risk into the false lumen and pericardium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)

options.text: Perform urgent pericardiocentesis for the moderate pericardial effusion demonstrated on the CT aortogram before any medical or surgical intervention is undertaken
options.rationale: Pericardiocentesis in Type A dissection without tamponade is contraindicated because it can precipitate haemodynamic collapse from re-bleeding into the pericardium. Definitive treatment is emergency cardiothoracic surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - Aortic dissection)

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection needs impulse control before pressure control: rate-limiting beta blocker first to blunt wall shear stress, then vasodilator to bring systolic blood pressure under 120 mmHg (measured in the higher arm). Emergency cardiothoracic surgery is definitive. Thrombolysis is contraindicated despite stroke features, which reflect innominate branch involvement rather than thromboembolic stroke.
key_points: Beta blocker FIRST for impulse control (target heart rate under 60), THEN vasodilator (target systolic under 120)
Thrombolysis and anticoagulation are contraindicated
Pericardiocentesis contraindicated in dissection with pericardial effusion without tamponade; if tamponade, only minimal drainage to restore perfusion until surgical repair
explanation.pearls: Measure blood pressure in the higher-reading arm to avoid under-treating on a compromised limb. A pulse deficit alone does not mean systemic hypotension.

sources.label: ANZ Society for Vascular Surgery Aortic Dissection Statement

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection despite borderline LRINEC
stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin presents with a 24-hour history of severe left lower leg pain following a minor gardening scratch 3 days ago. The pain is disproportionate to the visible skin findings, which show a 6 cm area of erythema with poorly demarcated edges and a small area of dusky violaceous discolouration in the centre. There is subcutaneous crepitus on palpation of the medial calf. He appears systemically unwell with a temperature of 38.6 degrees and rigors.

His white cell count is 16 x10 to the 9 per litre, C-reactive protein 180 mg/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, glucose 12 mmol/L (previous HbA1c 8.4 percent), and haemoglobin 138 g/L. His LRINEC score today is 6 (borderline: 6 to 7 indicates intermediate risk, 8 or above indicates high risk). Plain radiograph of the calf shows subcutaneous gas along the fascial planes. Blood cultures are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 122, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180), white cell count 16 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), CRP 180 mg/L (less than 5), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 12 mmol/L, LRINEC score 6
data_table.Imaging: plain radiograph left calf with subcutaneous gas along fascial planes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Await magnetic resonance imaging of the calf before proceeding to any operative intervention to define fascial involvement and target debridement extent precisely
options.rationale: MRI is helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain but must NOT delay surgery when clinical and plain radiographic features are already diagnostic. Delay is directly associated with mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin monotherapy at 2 g every 6 hours for community-acquired cellulitis and mark the area of erythema for reassessment in 6 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy is inadequate for polymicrobial necrotising soft tissue infection and does not provide toxin suppression. Marking and observation misses the operative window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: Activate the emergency theatre pathway for urgent surgical exploration and debridement while starting empirical intravenous meropenem plus clindamycin and resuscitation
options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a clinical and radiological diagnosis. The combination of pain out of proportion, dusky violaceous skin, subcutaneous crepitus, and radiological subcutaneous gas is highly specific despite a borderline LRINEC score. LRINEC has poor negative predictive value and should never delay surgery. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin (for toxin suppression) are given IMMEDIATELY but do not substitute for surgical debridement, which is the only definitive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: Repeat the LRINEC score in 6 hours and defer surgical exploration if the score remains below 8, using oral doxycycline for outpatient management in the meantime
options.rationale: LRINEC is a decision-aid not a rule-out tool. A borderline or low score does not exclude necrotising fasciitis with high pretest probability. Delaying surgery is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

options.text: Administer intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line empirical monotherapy for suspected streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and observe for haemodynamic response over 2 hours
options.rationale: IVIG has an adjunctive role in streptococcal toxic shock syndrome once diagnosis is confirmed but does not replace surgery and antibiotics as first-line management of necrotising soft tissue infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is diagnosed clinically and radiologically; the LRINEC score has poor negative predictive value and cannot rule it out when pretest probability is high (pain out of proportion, dusky skin, crepitus, and radiological gas are highly specific). Immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics with clindamycin (for toxin suppression) plus urgent surgical debridement are life-saving. Delay to imaging or scoring re-check increases mortality substantially.
key_points: High pretest probability features: pain out of proportion, dusky skin, crepitus, systemic toxicity, radiological subcutaneous gas
LRINEC is a decision-aid not a rule-out; borderline or low scores do not exclude the diagnosis
Empirical AU antibiotics: meropenem OR piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin for toxin suppression (add vancomycin if MRSA risk)
explanation.pearls: The clinical triage rule: if you are consulting surgery about NSTI, you are probably right. Delay to imaging is the commonest fatal error.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Necrotising soft tissue infection
Stevens et al. IDSA Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

stem:
A 52-year-old man with a history of intravenous methamphetamine use presents with three weeks of malaise, drenching night sweats and progressive dyspnoea. He describes cough with intermittent haemoptysis. He has never had rheumatic fever and had no known murmur previously.

He was febrile in triage. Transthoracic echocardiogram in ED shows a 12 mm mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve with moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Three sets of peripheral blood cultures drawn 30 minutes apart are all positive for Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin sensitive).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge increasing with inspiration; needle track marks in left cubital fossa; small vasculitic peripheral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures 3 of 3 positive Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin sensitive); CRP 240 mg/L (below 5); WCC 18.4 x10^9/L; chest x-ray with bilateral peripheral cavitating nodules

lead_in: How does this case classify under the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Rejected endocarditis pending transoesophageal echocardiography confirmation
options.rationale: Rejected requires firm alternative diagnosis or resolution with 4 days of antibiotics; this case is not rejected. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Definite endocarditis by two major criteria; empirical benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin therapy
options.rationale: Two major criteria (typical organism in two or more separate cultures plus positive echo with vegetation) equals definite endocarditis; empiric flucloxacillin (or benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending sensitivities) is standard. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Possible endocarditis by one major and one minor criterion needing additional imaging
options.rationale: This case fulfils two major criteria, not one; upgraded to definite classification. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)

options.text: Definite endocarditis by one major and three minor criteria requiring valve replacement
options.rationale: This route is a valid one for definite but not the classification here; two majors already suffice. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)

options.text: Rejected endocarditis; treat as suspected pulmonary emboli with anticoagulation cover only
options.rationale: The pulmonary nodules represent septic emboli from tricuspid endocarditis, not primary thromboembolic disease. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria define definite endocarditis with either (a) pathological criteria (culture or histology from vegetation or intracardiac abscess); (b) two major clinical criteria; (c) one major plus three minor; or (d) five minor. Major criteria are: typical organism in two or more separate blood cultures (or persistently positive) and evidence of endocardial involvement on echocardiography. Minor criteria include predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena, and microbiological evidence not meeting major. For IVDU tricuspid endocarditis, MSSA is most common; treatment is IV flucloxacillin 2 g four hourly for 2 to 6 weeks; TOE preferred over TTE for prosthetic valves and unclear TTE.
key_points: Duke: 2 majors, or 1 major + 3 minors, or 5 minors = definite.
IVDU tricuspid endocarditis most commonly MSSA.
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV 4 hourly for MSSA endocarditis.
TOE preferred to TTE for prosthetic valves or negative TTE with high suspicion.
explanation.pearls: Duke definite endocarditis by 2 major criteria: any typical organism in 2 or more separate cultures plus vegetation on echo; do not need pathology for the definite label.

sources.label: BSAC Duke criteria and endocarditis guidelines

stem:
A 68-year-old man presents to ED with a two-day history of severe headache, vomiting and fever, brought in by his wife. He has been progressively drowsy over the last six hours. He is a heavy smoker with COPD and has diet-controlled type 2 diabetes.

On arrival his GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5). He has neck stiffness and a positive Kernig's sign. He has no focal neurological deficit. His pupils are equal at 3 mm and briskly reactive. There is no petechial rash.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12; neck stiffness; Kernig positive; no focal deficit; no papilloedema on fundoscopy; no petechiae
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 340 mg/L (below 5); coags within normal limits; blood glucose 8.4 mmol/L; blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment before lumbar puncture?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and vancomycin 25 mg/kg targeting community meningitis pathogens
options.rationale: Missing benzylpenicillin misses Listeria cover which is essential above age 50 or in immunocompromised patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g and gentamicin 5 mg/kg empirically for suspected bacterial meningitis
options.rationale: This regimen misses ceftriaxone or cefotaxime which are cornerstone empiric cover for pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg targeting anaerobic and gram-negative cover
options.rationale: Metronidazole is not required for community meningitis and misses Listeria; benzylpenicillin plus a third generation cephalosporin is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg then ceftriaxone 2 g plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g four hourly
options.rationale: eTG empiric bacterial meningitis above age 50: dexamethasone 10 mg with or before first antibiotic dose, then ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (Listeria cover). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Wait for lumbar puncture and CT brain results before starting empirical antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Antibiotics should not be delayed beyond 30 minutes for imaging or LP when meningitis is suspected; give empirically then image. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Empiric adult bacterial meningitis therapy in Australia is dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily (or cefotaxime 2 g IV six hourly) for pneumococcal and meningococcal cover, plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV four hourly for Listeria cover in patients over 50, immunocompromised, or with alcohol use. If suspected penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, add vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg. Dexamethasone reduces neurological sequelae and mortality in pneumococcal meningitis. LP should not delay antibiotics; CT before LP only if focal deficit, GCS reduction, seizure, or immunocompromise.
key_points: Empiric therapy above age 50: ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin plus dexamethasone.
Vancomycin added if penicillin-resistant pneumococcus suspected.
Dexamethasone before or with first antibiotic dose.
Do not delay antibiotics for imaging or LP.
explanation.pearls: Empiric adult meningitis above age 50: dexamethasone 10 mg IV, ceftriaxone 2 g IV BD, plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV four hourly for Listeria cover.

stem:
A 68-year-old post-menopausal woman presents to her GP for routine review. She has no personal history of fragility fractures but her mother sustained a hip fracture at age 78. She takes no medications. She had menopause at age 51 and has never been on hormone therapy. She drinks two standard drinks daily on average.

Her BMI is 22 kg/m2 and she walks 30 minutes daily. Her recent DXA scan showed femoral neck T-score -2.8 and lumbar spine T-score -2.4. Her calculated 10-year FRAX major osteoporotic fracture risk is 22 percent and hip fracture risk is 6 percent (Australian tool with BMD input).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; height 162 cm (was 165 cm at age 50); no thoracic kyphosis; no tenderness to spinal percussion; no proximal myopathy
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L (within normal limits); vitamin D 68 nmol/L (above 50); TSH within normal limits; eGFR 74 mL/min/1.73 m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous every six months as first-line osteoporosis therapy
options.rationale: Denosumab is second-line under PBS after bisphosphonate intolerance or failure; oral alendronate is first-line for standard osteoporosis. (Source: RACGP: Osteoporosis; PBS criteria)

options.text: Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenous annually as first-line for post-menopausal osteoporosis
options.rationale: IV zoledronic acid is used for patients unable to tolerate or absorb oral bisphosphonate; not first-line without contraindication to oral. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Management)

options.text: Raloxifene 60 mg oral daily targeting spine fracture prevention in this post-menopausal woman
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral fracture but not hip fracture; not first-line when hip fracture prevention is a priority. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Management)

options.text: Teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneous daily for 18 months with strict PBS criteria compliance
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with prior minimal-trauma fractures under strict PBS criteria; not first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Management)

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg oral weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Oral alendronate is first-line PBS-subsidised bisphosphonate for post-menopausal osteoporosis with T-score below -2.5 or high fracture risk. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Management)

explanation.summary: Post-menopausal osteoporosis is treated with lifestyle measures (weight bearing exercise, alcohol and smoking reduction, adequate calcium 1000 to 1300 mg daily and vitamin D above 50 nmol/L) and pharmacotherapy when T-score is -2.5 or lower, or when there is a minimal trauma fracture. PBS first-line is oral alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly for at least 5 years. Zoledronic acid IV annually is for oral intolerance. Denosumab is second-line and requires strict continuation because of rebound vertebral fracture on cessation. Teriparatide is reserved for severe disease with prior fractures. Calcium and vitamin D adequacy should precede all antiresorptive therapy.
key_points: T-score -2.5 or below or fragility fracture triggers pharmacotherapy.
Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate) is first-line.
Denosumab needs strict continuation to avoid rebound fractures.
Ensure calcium and vitamin D adequacy first.
explanation.pearls: First-line post-menopausal osteoporosis: oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium 1000 to 1300 mg and vitamin D above 50 nmol/L; denosumab is second-line under PBS.

stem:
A 72-year-old man presents from a nursing home with two days of increasing confusion, dysuria and fever. On arrival to ED he is peripherally cool with capillary refill of 4 seconds. He has diet-controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension on perindopril.

After 30 mL/kg of intravenous crystalloid over 45 minutes his MAP is 58 mmHg and his lactate is 4.2 mmol/L (down from 5.1 on arrival). Urine dip shows leucocytes and nitrites. Blood cultures were drawn before piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g was started at the 30 minute mark. He has not passed urine in six hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 88/44 mmHg (MAP 58), respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert but drowsy, GCS 13; cool peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; soft abdomen with suprapubic tenderness; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L post-resuscitation; blood cultures pending; WCC 22.4 x10^9/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 92); potassium 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Give another 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassess in 15 minutes before starting vasopressor
options.rationale: After 30 mL/kg without target MAP achievement, further volume risks fluid overload; noradrenaline is Surviving Sepsis first-line vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ANZICS)

options.text: Change perindopril to intravenous dihydralazine to improve renal perfusion
options.rationale: Vasodilators worsen septic shock; the priority is vasoconstriction to restore MAP above 65 mmHg. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Start noradrenaline peripheral infusion via large vein while arranging central venous access
options.rationale: MAP under 65 mmHg despite 30 mL/kg fluid meets Surviving Sepsis criteria for vasopressor; noradrenaline is first-line and can start peripherally via large vein. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021; ANZICS)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg per day continuous infusion for refractory septic shock
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when vasopressor requirement is significant despite adequate resuscitation, not before starting vasopressor. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Change antibiotics to meropenem 1 g IV eight hourly for broader spectrum sepsis cover
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is appropriate empiric cover for urosepsis; the immediate problem is haemodynamic failure requiring vasopressor. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad spectrum antibiotics, start 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and apply vasopressors if MAP under 65 mmHg during or after fluid resuscitation. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; can start via a large peripheral vein while central access is being placed. Vasopressin is added second, then hydrocortisone for refractory shock. Bicarbonate is not used for pH above 7.15. Reassess lactate clearance to guide response.
key_points: 30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 hours for hypotension or lactate above 4.
MAP target 65 mmHg; noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor.
Peripheral noradrenaline via large vein permitted while central sited.
Hydrocortisone for refractory vasopressor-requiring shock.
explanation.pearls: After 30 mL/kg crystalloid with persistent MAP under 65 mmHg, start noradrenaline peripherally via a large vein without waiting for central access.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents with a 48-hour history of vomiting, abdominal pain and progressive weakness. She has known Addison's disease diagnosed three years ago and takes hydrocortisone 10 mg morning, 5 mg afternoon and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. She has not been able to keep tablets down for 24 hours.

She reports a fever and cough for four days before the vomiting started. She is normally well and her most recent endocrinology review last month was unremarkable. She carries an emergency injection kit but has not used it.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but responsive; dry mucous membranes; hyperpigmented palmar creases; capillary refill 4 seconds; abdomen soft with generalised tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), glucose 3.4 mmol/L (below 4.0), urea 11.2 mmol/L; VBG pH 7.30, HCO3 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and start 0.9 percent sodium chloride resuscitation
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis mandates immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM plus rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation; do not delay for confirmatory tests. (Source: Endocrine Society; RACGP; AMH)

options.text: Wait for 09:00 cortisol result and Synacthen stimulation before hydrocortisone administration
options.rationale: Diagnostic testing must not delay treatment of established adrenal crisis; give hydrocortisone first, then investigate. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg because it does not interfere with cortisol assay
options.rationale: Dexamethasone provides only glucocorticoid effect and no mineralocorticoid activity; hydrocortisone is preferred in known Addison's crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous insulin plus dextrose for the hyperkalaemia and delay steroid to after correction
options.rationale: Insulin and dextrose worsen hypoglycaemia and delay glucocorticoid; hyperkalaemia resolves with hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose today and admit for overnight observation
options.rationale: Oral therapy is unreliable in a vomiting hypotensive patient; adrenal crisis requires parenteral hydrocortisone immediately. (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and shock in an adrenally insufficient patient. Immediate treatment is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM followed by 200 mg per 24 hours (either as 50 mg every 6 hours IV or as an infusion) plus rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation. Precipitating illness (often infection or GI illness that prevents oral intake) needs concurrent treatment. Patients on chronic glucocorticoid replacement need sick-day rules: doubling oral hydrocortisone during minor illness, using parenteral hydrocortisone if unable to take oral, and going to hospital for vomiting despite injection. Prescribe injectable hydrocortisone emergency kit to all patients.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately.
Follow with 200 mg per 24 hours plus isotonic fluid.
Do not delay for cortisol or Synacthen results.
Sick-day rules: double oral, parenteral if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: Suspected adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM plus 0.9 percent sodium chloride immediately; investigate afterwards, not before treatment.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with a 24-hour history of severe left thigh pain that started after a minor trampoline injury with his grandchildren. He describes the pain as out of proportion to what the skin looks like, and it has escalated from moderate to unbearable overnight. He looks unwell.

Examination shows a swollen left thigh with tenderness extending well beyond the erythematous area. There is dusky skin discolouration medially with two small bullae, and crepitus is palpable on the anterior thigh. The overlying skin is warm but not obviously fluctuant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left thigh with dusky discolouration medially, two small bullae, crepitus anteriorly; pain out of proportion to visual signs; peripheral pulses present
data_table.Investigations: CRP 320 mg/L (below 5); WCC 24.6 x10^9/L; sodium 133 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88); glucose 14.8 mmol/L; haemoglobin 108 g/L (130 to 180); LRINEC score 11

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g four hourly and mark erythema border for 6 hourly review
options.rationale: Cellulitis therapy alone with border marking delays surgical debridement, which is the definitive treatment; mortality rises sharply with delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZ Society of Vascular Surgery)

options.text: Emergency surgical debridement with concurrent broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: LRINEC 8 or above with clinical features (pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, dusky skin) is necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgery within 6 hours is life-saving. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as monotherapy before considering surgical debridement
options.rationale: HBO is an adjunct only; surgical debridement plus antibiotics is primary treatment and should not be delayed for HBO. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Bedside incision and drainage under local anaesthetic in the emergency department
options.rationale: Bedside I and D is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis; theatre debridement to viable tissue with wide excision is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Wait for MRI imaging with gadolinium confirmation before proceeding to theatre for surgery
options.rationale: Imaging delays lifesaving surgery when clinical suspicion is high; go directly to theatre based on clinical and LRINEC findings. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis features pain out of proportion to visible signs, rapid progression, systemic sepsis, dusky skin, bullae, and crepitus. LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose; a score of 6 or above raises suspicion, 8 or above strongly predicts. Definitive management is emergency surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics (typically meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin) and ICU support. Delayed surgery is the strongest predictor of mortality. Imaging must not delay theatre when clinical suspicion is high. Group A streptococcus, Clostridium and polymicrobial infection are common causes.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, dusky skin.
LRINEC 8 or above strongly predicts.
Emergency debridement within 6 hours plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Do not delay surgery for imaging.
explanation.pearls: Necrotising fasciitis with LRINEC 8 or above: theatre for wide debridement within 6 hours, meropenem plus clindamycin plus vancomycin, do not wait for imaging.

sources.label: ANZ Society for Vascular Surgery: Necrotising soft tissue infection

stem:
An 82-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin only is brought in by his son with two weeks of increasing confusion. He has drunk less than usual because he lives alone and thinks his son forgot to bring water. He has no chest pain or focal deficit but is very drowsy on arrival.

His capillary glucose meter reads high (above 33). Formal glucose is 62 mmol/L. His son reports no polyuria historically. He has not vomited and has no abdominal pain. He was independent in his own home four weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12; dry mucous membranes; tenting skin turgor; no ketotic breath; abdomen soft; no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 62 mmol/L, ketones 0.9 mmol/L, sodium 156 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 28 mmol/L, creatinine 220 micromol/L, VBG pH 7.32, HCO3 20 mmol/L, calculated osmolality 380 mOsm/kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 500 mL bolus and start insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately
options.rationale: In HHS insulin is delayed until fluid alone has brought glucose down 5 mmol/L per hour; immediate insulin risks cerebral oedema and cardiovascular collapse. (Source: JBDS-IP HHS; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous Hartmann's 20 mL/kg bolus then insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour after 2 hours
options.rationale: Hartmann's carries potassium load; JBDS uses 0.9 percent sodium chloride first-line for HHS with slow controlled rehydration. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)

options.text: Intravenous 0.45 percent sodium chloride at 250 mL per hour without any insulin therapy
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid drops osmolality too fast in the first hour; 0.9 percent NaCl first, switch to 0.45 percent later if osmolality falls too slowly. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 250 mL bolus then 5 percent dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hour
options.rationale: Adding dextrose before glucose falls below 14 mmol/L slows correction; do not add glucose in the first hours of HHS. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 litre over 1 hour then reassess before starting insulin
options.rationale: JBDS HHS pathway starts with 1 litre 0.9 percent NaCl over 1 hour, targeting glucose fall of 5 mmol/L per hour by fluid alone; insulin only if glucose is not falling. (Source: JBDS Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State)

explanation.summary: HHS is characterised by marked hyperglycaemia (usually above 30 mmol/L), hyperosmolality (above 320 mOsm/kg), and volume depletion without significant ketosis or acidosis. Fluid resuscitation is the mainstay: 1 litre 0.9 percent NaCl over 1 hour then 0.5 to 1 litre per hour for several hours, targeting glucose fall of 5 mmol/L per hour and sodium fall not exceeding 10 mmol/L in 24 hours. Insulin is delayed until glucose stops falling with fluid alone or ketones rise; a low dose (0.05 units/kg/hour) is used. Potassium replacement follows the same criteria as DKA. Complications include cerebral oedema (from rapid osmolar shifts), central pontine myelinolysis (from rapid sodium correction), and thromboembolism (heparin prophylaxis is standard). Mortality is 10 to 20 percent, higher than DKA.
key_points: HHS: glucose above 30, osmolality above 320, minimal ketosis.
First hour: 1 L 0.9 percent NaCl; do not start insulin yet.
Target glucose fall 5 mmol/L per hour by fluid alone.
Insulin 0.05 units/kg/hour only when glucose stops falling.
explanation.pearls: HHS first hour: 1 L 0.9 percent NaCl alone, no insulin until glucose fall stalls; unlike DKA, insulin is not part of the initial resuscitation because fluid alone typically drops glucose adequately.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is brought to a regional ED after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. She has a distended abdomen with generalised tenderness and a suspected pelvic fracture on FAST-positive imaging. She has already received 1 litre of 0.9 percent sodium chloride and 1 unit of O negative packed red cells.

Her initial haemoglobin was 82 g/L (115 to 165) and lactate 5.4 mmol/L. Her INR just returned at 1.8. The retrieval team is 45 minutes away. She has just received 4 units of packed red cells across the last 20 minutes and is still bleeding actively.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 96 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 35.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13; pelvic binder in place; distended tender abdomen; peripheral cool with capillary refill 5 seconds; ongoing large-volume bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 82 g/L; INR 1.8; platelet 108 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 1.6 g/L (2.0 to 4.0); ionised calcium 1.02 mmol/L (1.15 to 1.30); lactate 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combined next management step?

options.text: Continue packed red cells only until INR corrects below 1.5 before adding fresh frozen plasma
options.rationale: Waiting until INR corrects worsens dilutional coagulopathy; MTP delivers RBC, FFP and platelets in balanced ratio from activation. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion; ANZICS)

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g only and continue packed red cells as the next step
options.rationale: TXA is essential but is not sufficient; ongoing haemorrhage with hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis warrants full MTP activation. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)

options.text: Give warm crystalloid 2 litres and elevate legs to increase preload before further blood products
options.rationale: Crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy; blood product ratio therapy is preferred with permissive hypotension. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)

options.text: Activate MTP with RBC to FFP to platelets 1:1:1, tranexamic acid 1 g, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen
options.rationale: Ongoing bleeding after 4 units RBC with coagulopathy, hypothermia, acidosis triggers MTP; 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA plus cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen below 2. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)

options.text: Give prothrombin complex concentrate 25 units/kg to correct INR before further transfusion
options.rationale: PCC is reserved for warfarin or DOAC reversal, not trauma coagulopathy; balanced blood product ratio is the primary strategy. (Source: NBA: Massive Transfusion)

explanation.summary: MTP is activated when massive haemorrhage is anticipated (typically more than 4 units of RBC in 1 hour, or expected total more than 10 units in 24 hours, or as clinically triggered by ongoing bleeding with coagulopathy). Products are delivered in balanced ratio (RBC to FFP to platelets 1:1:1) to prevent dilutional coagulopathy. Adjuncts: tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2), cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate to keep fibrinogen above 1.5 to 2.0 g/L, calcium replacement to keep ionised calcium above 1.1 mmol/L (citrate binds calcium), warming to prevent the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy. Damage control resuscitation targets permissive hypotension (systolic 80 to 90 mmHg) until surgical control.
key_points: MTP: RBC:FFP:platelets 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA plus cryoprecipitate.
Tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2).
Keep fibrinogen above 1.5, ionised calcium above 1.1.
Permissive hypotension until surgical control.
explanation.pearls: Trauma MTP activation criteria: ongoing bleeding, 4 units RBC in 1 hour, INR above 1.5 or fibrinogen below 2, hypothermia below 35 degrees; deliver 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA plus cryoprecipitate from the outset.

subtopic_detail: Right-sided endocarditis in an IV drug user
stem:
A 32-year-old man with a history of intravenous heroin use presents with 5 days of fevers to 39.5 degrees, rigors, and a dry cough with mild pleuritic chest pain. He last injected 8 days ago. On examination he is warm and diaphoretic with tender needle-track marks in the left antecubital fossa. Chest auscultation is clear. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge that varies with respiration.

He is hepatitis C positive and untreated, HIV negative on testing 6 months ago. Chest X-ray shows scattered bilateral peripheral rounded infiltrates. Blood cultures have been drawn from two separate sites.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; needle-track marks left antecubital fossa; soft tricuspid systolic murmur that varies with respiration; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 210 mg/L (<5); troponin within normal limits; chest X-ray: bilateral peripheral rounded infiltrates; ECG sinus tachycardia; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours plus vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose
options.rationale: Right-sided IE in an IV drug user is usually Staphylococcus aureus; empirical therapy targets MSSA and MRSA together (flucloxacillin plus vancomycin) until sensitivities are known. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 4 to 5 mg/kg daily
options.rationale: This is the empirical regimen for native-valve left-sided community-onset endocarditis without staphylococcal risk factors; it undertreats staphylococcal disease in an IV drug user. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus rifampicin as outpatient management now
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inappropriate for endocarditis; parenteral therapy is required until bactericidal control is documented. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 hours plus gentamicin daily
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam does not adequately cover MRSA and is not the standard empirical regimen for IE; staphylococcal cover is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily as monotherapy pending culture and echocardiography
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover staphylococci adequately and misses MRSA in an IV drug user population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Right-sided infective endocarditis in an IV drug user is characteristically caused by Staphylococcus aureus and typically involves the tricuspid valve with septic pulmonary emboli on chest imaging. Australian empirical therapy targets both MSSA and MRSA pending culture results: flucloxacillin plus vancomycin (loading dose then weight-based maintenance). Once organism and sensitivities are known, therapy is narrowed: flucloxacillin monotherapy for MSSA, vancomycin monotherapy for MRSA. Duration is at least 4 weeks IV for uncomplicated right-sided IE, longer for complications. Echocardiography (transthoracic first, transoesophageal if inconclusive or valve surgery being considered) is essential.
key_points: Right-sided IE in IVDU is usually Staph aureus.
Empirical cover: flucloxacillin plus vancomycin for MSSA and MRSA.
Narrow to flucloxacillin (MSSA) or vancomycin (MRSA) on sensitivities.
Uncomplicated right-sided IE requires 4 weeks IV therapy.
explanation.pearls: In an IV drug user with fevers, pulmonary infiltrates and a tricuspid murmur, start empirical flucloxacillin plus vancomycin after two sets of blood cultures; do not use ceftriaxone monotherapy or oral therapy.

stem:
A 26-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic 12 days after a condomless receptive anal sex encounter with a new partner of unknown HIV status. He has had a febrile illness for 4 days with pharyngitis, myalgias, headache and a fine truncal maculopapular rash. He denies genital ulcers. A rapid fourth-generation antibody-antigen combination assay in-clinic is negative. He has never previously been tested for HIV and has not taken PEP.

He has no significant medical history, is on no regular medications, and is otherwise well. He has already agreed to further testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fine truncal maculopapular rash; pharyngeal erythema without exudate; bilateral non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Fourth-generation HIV Ab-Ag combined assay negative; syphilis serology, hepatitis B/C serology, gonorrhoea and chlamydia PCR sent; monospot pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?

options.text: Repeat the fourth-generation antibody-antigen assay in 8 weeks after exposure
options.rationale: The clinical picture is highly suggestive of acute HIV seroconversion; waiting 8 weeks delays diagnosis while transmission risk is highest. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Order HIV Western blot confirmatory testing on the same sample tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Western blot detects antibody, which lags viral RNA; a negative combined assay implies Western blot would also be negative in the window period. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Order CD4 lymphocyte subset counts to look for a fall consistent with primary infection
options.rationale: CD4 counts are not diagnostic in acute infection; they are used for staging established disease and monitoring therapy. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Test for Epstein-Barr virus IgM antibody as most likely alternative cause of the rash
options.rationale: EBV remains a differential but does not rule out acute HIV; failing to test for HIV RNA in this clinical picture would miss primary infection. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Order HIV RNA (viral load) PCR now for detection during the antibody window period
options.rationale: HIV RNA becomes detectable around 10 days post-exposure, before p24 antigen and antibody; RNA is the diagnostic test during the antibody window in symptomatic seroconversion. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

explanation.summary: The Australian HIV testing algorithm during suspected acute seroconversion uses HIV RNA (viral load) PCR to detect infection during the antibody window period. Fourth-generation antibody-antigen combined assays detect p24 antigen from around 14 to 21 days post-exposure and antibody from 20 to 45 days. HIV RNA becomes detectable earliest, from around 10 days post-exposure. Symptomatic acute seroconversion presents with a mononucleosis-like illness (fever, pharyngitis, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia) and represents the period of highest transmission risk. Positive RNA testing should be followed by confirmatory testing and immediate linkage to specialist care and antiretroviral therapy initiation.
key_points: HIV RNA is detectable from around 10 days post-exposure.
Fourth-generation antibody-antigen from 2 to 3 weeks; antibody from 3 to 6 weeks.
Symptomatic seroconversion is the period of highest transmission risk.
Positive RNA triggers immediate linkage to specialist care.
explanation.pearls: In a mononucleosis-like illness with recent condomless anal sex and negative combined assay, order HIV RNA PCR immediately rather than waiting for antibody seroconversion.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV Medicine (ASHM) Guidelines

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of a red, swollen and exquisitely tender left lower leg after a minor gardening abrasion. Pain is severe and out of proportion to visible skin changes. There are patches of dusky discolouration in the calf and small tense bullae are developing. He has generalised systemic symptoms with rigors.

He last used insulin 8 hours ago. He has no known allergies. Bloods were drawn on arrival and IV access is established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Left calf red, hot, swollen with dusky patches and small tense bullae; exquisite tenderness; sensation reduced over lateral calf; distal pulses palpable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.8 x10^9/L (4-11), Hb 118 g/L (135-175), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 14.2 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (60-110), CRP 342 mg/L (<5), lactate 4.6 mmol/L; LRINEC score 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Elevate the leg and start oral flucloxacillin 500 mg 6-hourly with community follow-up
options.rationale: The presentation is high probability necrotising soft tissue infection (LRINEC 8); oral outpatient therapy is inappropriate and fatal delay is likely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.text: Immediate surgical review for urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
options.rationale: LRINEC score 6 or above is high probability necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement is the definitive treatment along with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue
