options.text: MRI leg with contrast to confirm fascial involvement before considering surgical review
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high; MRI has a role only if surgical decision is genuinely uncertain and delay is not harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone with ward observation and hourly review
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy misses gram-negative and anaerobic cover; NSTI requires triple-agent empirical therapy plus surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

options.text: Skin punch biopsy at the affected calf site for Gram stain and culture before treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy has no acute diagnostic role; deep tissue samples are taken intraoperatively. Delay to biopsy would be fatal in NSTI. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency and diagnosis is primarily clinical. Features raising suspicion include severe pain out of proportion, dusky skin changes, bullae, crepitus, cutaneous anaesthesia, systemic toxicity and rapid progression. The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose to stratify risk; score 6 or above is high probability of NSTI. Definitive treatment is early aggressive surgical debridement combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, plus vancomycin, plus clindamycin for toxin suppression). Imaging must not delay surgery.
key_points: Diagnosis of NSTI is clinical; LRINEC assists risk stratification.
LRINEC 6 or above is high probability.
Surgical debridement is definitive treatment.
Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: In a diabetic with pain out of proportion, dusky calf skin, bullae and LRINEC 6 or above, call the surgeon before you order the CT scan; delayed debridement is the leading cause of mortality.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Skin and soft tissue

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease is brought to ED by her partner with 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain and increasing lethargy after a gastroenteritis illness. She takes hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 5 mg at midday and 5 mg at 4pm, plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily. She has been unable to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose today. She is drowsy but rousable, feels dizzy on sitting, and looks pigmented.

Her partner reports that she did not double her hydrocortisone dose despite the illness. There is no fever and no localising infective source.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min supine, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg supine, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but oriented; hyperpigmented palmar creases; dry mucous membranes; abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), creatinine 132 micromol/L (60-110); venous gas pH 7.28, HCO3 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 50 mg with intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 250 mL/hour
options.rationale: Oral steroids are inappropriate when the patient is vomiting; parenteral hydrocortisone is required and prednisolone lacks the mineralocorticoid activity of hydrocortisone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: Increase fludrocortisone to 200 microgram orally and give oral rehydration solution
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not the acute treatment; glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone) is urgent and the patient is vomiting so oral therapy is inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: IV dexamethasone 4 mg with intravenous fluid resuscitation and glucose supplementation
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and hydrocortisone is preferred; dexamethasone is used only if the diagnosis is uncertain and short synacthen test is planned. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: IV noradrenaline infusion to restore blood pressure before hydrocortisone administration
options.rationale: Vasopressors are refractory to steroid deficiency; hydrocortisone must be given first and vasopressors are used only if BP remains inadequate after fluids and steroids. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg over 24 hours with intravenous fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours) alongside IV fluid resuscitation and glucose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology - Adrenal crisis)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency in known Addison's disease, often triggered by intercurrent illness or failure of sick-day dose adjustment. Immediate treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (either continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours), together with 1 litre of 0.9 percent sodium chloride over the first hour and glucose replacement for hypoglycaemia. Hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and adequate mineralocorticoid activity at these doses so separate fludrocortisone is not needed until doses drop below 50 mg per day. Patients should be educated on sick-day rules (double oral dose for febrile illness, IM hydrocortisone if vomiting).
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity at these doses.
IV fluids: 1 litre 0.9 percent sodium chloride in the first hour.
Sick-day rules: double oral dose or IM hydrocortisone if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: In known Addison's disease with vomiting and hypotension, give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately and 1 litre normal saline in the first hour before any workup; dexamethasone is reserved for undiagnosed cases going for synacthen testing.

stem:
A 44-year-old man presents to ED with 5 days of ascending symmetric limb weakness that started with distal paraesthesia in the feet. He is now unable to walk unaided and has weakness in his shoulder girdle. He had gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago. His forced vital capacity at the bedside is 22 mL/kg (predicted 60 mL/kg). Reflexes are absent at the ankles and knees and reduced in the upper limbs.

Swallow is intact at bedside review. Cranial nerve examination is normal apart from a mild bilateral facial weakness. He has no bladder or bowel dysfunction.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symmetric flaccid limb weakness power 3/5 lower limbs, 4/5 upper limbs; absent lower limb and reduced upper limb reflexes; bilateral facial weakness; sensation reduced to pinprick distally
data_table.Investigations: CSF: protein 0.98 g/L (0.15-0.45), WCC 3/mm3, glucose within normal limits; nerve conduction studies show reduced motor amplitudes with prolonged distal latencies; FVC 22 mL/kg predicted 60

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunotherapy?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days followed by oral prednisolone
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective in Guillain-Barre syndrome and may worsen outcomes; IVIG or plasma exchange are the treatments of choice. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days with respiratory monitoring
options.rationale: IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days is equivalent to plasma exchange in accelerating recovery when started within 4 weeks of onset; IVIG is generally preferred for ease of administration and availability. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

options.text: Combined IVIG and plasma exchange sequentially over 2 weeks with steroid cover
options.rationale: Combining IVIG and PLEX does not improve outcomes over either alone and increases cost and complications; single-modality therapy is standard. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

options.text: Oral azathioprine 2 mg/kg daily with weekly IVIG boosters for 3 to 6 months
options.rationale: Long-term immunosuppression is used for chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), not acute GBS; acute treatment is short-course IVIG or PLEX. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

options.text: Supportive care alone with high dependency unit observation and physiotherapy support
options.rationale: Supportive care alone underserves patients with rapidly progressive disease or respiratory compromise; immunotherapy shortens recovery time and reduces disability. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Guillain-Barre)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome is treated with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, both of which shorten recovery when given within 4 weeks of symptom onset. Neither corticosteroids alone nor a combination of IVIG and PLEX improve outcomes. Australian standard therapy is IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days. Respiratory monitoring is critical: forced vital capacity under 20 mL/kg, negative inspiratory force weaker than -30 cmH2O or vital capacity fall over 30 percent from baseline signal impending respiratory failure and are indications for early ICU transfer and elective intubation. Autonomic instability and dysautonomia must be watched for.
key_points: IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days is equivalent to PLEX.
Steroids are not effective in acute GBS.
FVC under 20 mL/kg triggers ICU and intubation consideration.
Autonomic dysfunction is common; continuous cardiac monitoring required.
explanation.pearls: In GBS with FVC under 25 mL/kg, start IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days and transfer to a monitored bed; steroids do not help and combined IVIG plus PLEX offers no advantage.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to rheumatology outpatients with 10 weeks of symmetric small joint pain and morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes. On examination there is tender synovitis in 8 metacarpophalangeal joints and both wrists. Rheumatoid factor is positive at 108 IU/mL and anti-CCP is positive at over 200 U/mL. CRP is elevated at 52 mg/L. She has no significant medical history and does not drink alcohol.

Hand X-rays are normal without erosions. She has no plans for pregnancy and is currently using an intrauterine device. She has no active infection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral symmetric MCP and wrist synovitis; DAS28 5.4; no rheumatoid nodules; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: RF 108 IU/mL (<15), anti-CCP over 200 U/mL, CRP 52 mg/L (<5), ESR 68 mm/hr; LFTs, U and E, hepatitis B/C, TB QuantiFERON, chest X-ray all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial DMARD?

options.text: Sulfasalazine 500 mg twice daily titrating slowly to 2 g daily over 4 weeks
options.rationale: Sulfasalazine is a DMARD alternative for methotrexate-intolerant or pregnancy-planning patients; it is not the standard first-line agent when methotrexate is safe. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily as sole disease-modifying therapy at start
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine monotherapy is inadequate for moderate to high disease activity; methotrexate is preferred as first-line. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

options.text: Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks as first-line biologic monotherapy now
options.rationale: Biologics are used after inadequate response to conventional DMARDs; PBS eligibility requires demonstrated failure of methotrexate plus at least one other conventional DMARD. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

options.text: Methotrexate 15 mg orally once weekly with folic acid 5 mg once weekly the next day
options.rationale: Australian consensus (ARA) makes methotrexate first-line for RA when there is no contraindication; starting dose 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg on a different day reduces gastrointestinal and mucosal side effects. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

options.text: Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily long-term as monotherapy until disease remission achieved
options.rationale: Chronic corticosteroid monotherapy is not disease-modifying long-term and carries significant harms; steroids may be used as short-term bridge alongside DMARD initiation. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association Consensus)

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is first-line disease-modifying therapy for rheumatoid arthritis in Australia when there is no contraindication. Starting dose is 10 to 15 mg orally once weekly, escalated to 20 to 25 mg weekly as tolerated over 8 to 12 weeks, with folic acid 5 mg weekly on a different day to reduce side effects. Pre-treatment screening covers hepatitis B and C serology, latent TB (QuantiFERON), liver function, renal function and chest X-ray. Bridging low-dose prednisolone may be used for symptomatic control during DMARD onset. Biologics are added when conventional DMARDs fail; PBS eligibility requires demonstrated failure of methotrexate and one other conventional DMARD.
key_points: Methotrexate is first-line RA DMARD in Australia.
Starting dose 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg different day.
Pre-screen: hepatitis B/C, QuantiFERON, LFT, U/E, CXR.
Biologics after conventional DMARD failure per PBS criteria.
explanation.pearls: For new RA with high disease activity and no contraindication, start methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg on a different day; biologics come only after conventional DMARD failure under PBS rules.

stem:
An 82-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents by ambulance with a 6-hour history of confusion, right-sided weakness and headache after a fall. CT brain shows a 25 mL left frontoparietal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 3 mm midline shift. Her INR on arrival is 4.2. Her weight is 68 kg. She is drowsy but rousable with a Glasgow Coma Score of 12.

She takes no other anticoagulant, has stable renal function and no known allergies to vitamin K or blood products. Neurosurgery has been contacted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 172/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5); right-sided facial droop and 3/5 weakness in the right arm; pupils equal and reactive; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: INR 4.2 (target 2-3); creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110); platelets 240 x10^9/L; CT: 25 mL left frontoparietal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 3 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg orally with fresh frozen plasma 4 units and 6-hourly INR checks
options.rationale: Oral vitamin K is too slow (12 to 24 hours) and FFP is slower and less effective than prothrombinex-VF for warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage; IV vitamin K and prothrombinex-VF are indicated. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg without vitamin K and repeat INR after 4 hours
options.rationale: FFP is second-line reversal because volume load and time-to-normalise INR are inferior to prothrombinex-VF; vitamin K is also essential for durable reversal. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 g intravenously with intravenous vitamin K 10 mg co-administered
options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; it has no role here. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 40 microgram/kg with vitamin K 10 mg intravenously
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not standard warfarin reversal and carries thromboembolic risk; prothrombinex-VF is the preferred product for warfarin-related intracranial bleeding. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

options.text: Prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg intravenously plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg intravenously
options.rationale: For life-threatening warfarin-associated bleeding, Australian standard is prothrombinex-VF (three-factor PCC) 25 to 50 IU/kg IV plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV; FFP is added if factor VII replacement is needed for full correction. (Source: Australian Blood Authority: Warfarin reversal)

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, is reversed with intravenous vitamin K plus a prothrombin complex concentrate. In Australia, prothrombinex-VF (three-factor PCC containing factors II, IX and X) is the standard product, dosed at 25 to 50 IU/kg IV depending on the INR and clinical urgency, with concurrent IV vitamin K 5 to 10 mg for durable reversal. Fresh frozen plasma may be added if factor VII replacement is needed. Repeat INR is measured 30 to 60 minutes after prothrombinex-VF to confirm reversal. Definitive management includes blood pressure control (target systolic under 140 mmHg for spontaneous ICH per INTERACT2) and neurosurgical review.
key_points: Prothrombinex-VF 25 to 50 IU/kg plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV.
FFP is second-line or adjunct for factor VII replacement.
Vitamin K essential for durable reversal (short PCC half-life).
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses xabans.
explanation.pearls: In warfarin-associated ICH, give prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg plus IV vitamin K 10 mg immediately and control blood pressure to systolic under 140 mmHg; FFP alone or oral vitamin K is too slow.

stem:
A 58-year-old man had a proximal right femoral vein deep vein thrombosis 6 months ago with no identifiable provoking factor. He has been on apixaban 5 mg twice daily since diagnosis and has had no bleeding complications. Follow-up screening for cancer was negative, and thrombophilia screening was negative. He is well and asymptomatic today.

His HAS-BLED score is 1 (age over 65 not yet reached). Blood pressure is controlled and there is no history of GI bleeding, renal impairment or falls. He is fit and physically active.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well; no calf swelling or tenderness; no bruising; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: FBC and U and E within normal limits; creatinine clearance 82 mL/min; ferritin, iron studies and faecal occult blood negative; imaging follow-up 6 months post-DVT unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation today as the initial 6-month treatment course is now complete
options.rationale: Unprovoked proximal DVT carries a recurrence risk of around 10 percent in the first year and 30 percent at 5 years after stopping; indefinite anticoagulation is recommended unless bleeding risk is high. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely for continued VTE prevention
options.rationale: The AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD after 6 months, but this is one option; full-dose continuation is also acceptable. However indefinite continuation is what is indicated - the specific dose regimen is a secondary decision. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Continue indefinite anticoagulation; reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is preferred
options.rationale: For unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk, indefinite anticoagulation is recommended; reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD after the initial treatment period is supported by AMPLIFY-EXT and reduces recurrence with comparable bleeding to placebo. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Switch to aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely as extended prevention with lower bleeding risk
options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to reduced-dose apixaban for VTE recurrence prevention; it is an option only when anticoagulation is refused or contraindicated. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

options.text: Switch to warfarin with target INR 2 to 3 and cease DOAC use going forward
options.rationale: There is no advantage to switching from apixaban to warfarin unless there is a specific indication (mechanical valve, severe renal impairment); DOACs are preferred in Australian guidance for uncomplicated VTE. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - VTE)

explanation.summary: Unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis carries a substantial long-term recurrence risk (around 10 percent in the first year off treatment, 30 percent at 5 years) and Australian guidance supports indefinite anticoagulation unless the patient has high bleeding risk. Reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily after the initial 6 months of full-dose treatment is supported by the AMPLIFY-EXT trial and reduces recurrence with bleeding rates comparable to placebo. Full-dose continuation (apixaban 5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 20 mg daily) is also acceptable. Aspirin is inferior to apixaban but is an option when anticoagulation is refused or contraindicated. Reassessment of bleeding risk should be periodic.
key_points: Unprovoked proximal DVT recurrence: 10 percent in year 1 off Rx.
Indefinite anticoagulation recommended when bleeding risk is low.
Reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD after 6 months per AMPLIFY-EXT.
Aspirin is inferior to apixaban for extended prevention.
explanation.pearls: After 6 months for unprovoked proximal DVT, continue indefinite anticoagulation and consider stepping down to apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily; do not stop at 6 months and do not switch to aspirin.

A 68-year-old man presents with 3 months of nasal crusting, epistaxis, purpuric rash on the lower limbs and a 7 kg weight loss. He now has haemoptysis over the past week and shortness of breath on stairs. Creatinine has risen from 88 micromol/L six months ago to 262 micromol/L today. Urinalysis shows haematuria and proteinuria with red cell casts on microscopy. Chest CT shows patchy bilateral cavitating pulmonary nodules.

He has no active infection on screening. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, QuantiFERON and beta-D-glucan are negative. Kidney biopsy has been arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 152/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Purpuric palpable lesions on lower limbs; nasal crusting with a septal defect; chest with scattered coarse crackles bibasally
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 262 micromol/L (60-110), urine PCR 320 mg/mmol; c-ANCA positive with PR3 titre elevated; kidney biopsy pending; chest CT bilateral cavitating nodules; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction therapy?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily as monotherapy with hydroxychloroquine and calcium
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy is inadequate induction for severe ANCA vasculitis with organ-threatening disease; a cytotoxic agent or rituximab is required. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

options.text: Intravenous rituximab 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks plus glucocorticoid taper
options.rationale: Rituximab plus glucocorticoids is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide plus glucocorticoids for induction in severe ANCA vasculitis and is preferred where fertility preservation, prior cyclophosphamide exposure or PR3 positivity applies; RITUXVAS and RAVE support this. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

options.text: Plasma exchange every second day for 14 days as sole induction without steroid cover
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is an adjunct in severe pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis-dependent renal failure and is not standalone induction; PEXIVAS reduced enthusiasm for routine use. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

options.text: Oral cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg daily for 3 months with folate and steroid support
options.rationale: Oral cyclophosphamide is a legitimate induction regimen but is less used since rituximab became available; IV pulsed cyclophosphamide or rituximab is preferred to minimise cumulative toxicity. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

options.text: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folate and low-dose prednisolone as sole induction
options.rationale: Methotrexate is used for non-organ-threatening disease; it is inadequate for severe ANCA vasculitis with renal or pulmonary involvement. (Source: KDIGO Glomerulonephritis Guideline 2021)

explanation.summary: Severe ANCA-associated vasculitis with organ-threatening disease (renal, pulmonary, neurological) requires combination induction with a cytotoxic or biologic agent plus glucocorticoids. Rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks) plus glucocorticoids has become the preferred regimen in most centres based on RAVE and RITUXVAS; it is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide for induction and is preferred when fertility preservation matters, prior cyclophosphamide exposure exists, or in PR3-ANCA disease where relapse rates are higher and rituximab retreatment is more feasible. Plasma exchange is reserved for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis-dependent renal failure; PEXIVAS reduced routine indications. Maintenance is with rituximab or azathioprine.
key_points: Severe ANCA vasculitis requires combination induction, not steroid alone.
Rituximab plus steroid is at least equivalent to cyclophosphamide.
Rituximab preferred for fertility, prior cyclophosphamide, PR3 positivity.
Plasma exchange reserved for severe pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis need.
explanation.pearls: In new severe PR3-positive ANCA vasculitis with pulmonary-renal syndrome, induce with rituximab plus glucocorticoids rather than cyclophosphamide when fertility, prior exposure or relapse risk favours it.

A 72-year-old postmenopausal woman presents 4 weeks after a low-trauma T12 vertebral fracture confirmed on lateral thoracolumbar X-ray. She reports mild persisting back pain but is now mobilising with a physiotherapist. Her DXA scan today shows a T-score of -3.1 at the femoral neck and -3.4 at the lumbar spine. Her calcium is 2.28 mmol/L and vitamin D is 68 nmol/L. Renal function is normal.

She has no significant medical history and does not take steroids. She has good dentition, has not had recent dental extractions and has no planned dental procedures.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mild kyphosis, tender over T12; no proximal weakness; normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Investigations: DXA T-score femoral neck -3.1, lumbar spine -3.4; calcium 2.28 mmol/L (2.1-2.6), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L, PTH within normal limits, vitamin D 68 nmol/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L; FRAX 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk 32 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Oral calcium 1200 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU daily as sole therapy without antiresorptive
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D alone are inadequate for established osteoporosis with prevalent fragility fracture; antiresorptive therapy is required. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation ongoing
options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate weekly) is first-line for postmenopausal osteoporosis with fragility fracture; PBS-listed for T-score less than -2.5 or prior fracture. Denosumab is an alternative but requires strict compliance. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 microgram daily as first-line anabolic agent for 24 months
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for very severe osteoporosis or bisphosphonate/denosumab failure; PBS criteria require T-score less than -3.0 with at least two fractures despite antiresorptive therapy. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Oral raloxifene 60 mg daily as selective oestrogen receptor modulator therapy first
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not non-vertebral fracture risk and is second-line; VTE risk is a concern in older women. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months as monotherapy after single loading dose
options.rationale: Denosumab is an alternative first-line but strict 6-monthly compliance is essential; if a dose is missed by more than a month, rebound vertebral fracture risk rises. Oral bisphosphonate is preferred where compliance concerns exist. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Guideline)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture in Australia is oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly), backed by calcium and vitamin D. Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous every 6 months is an alternative but requires strict compliance because interrupting or ceasing denosumab causes rebound vertebral fractures within 12 months; if it must be stopped, a bisphosphonate is prescribed as bridge. Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly is used in adherence-limited patients. Teriparatide (an anabolic agent) is reserved for very severe osteoporosis or antiresorptive failure per PBS criteria. Duration of bisphosphonate is typically 3 to 5 years with a treatment pause thereafter if T-score improves and there is no fracture.
key_points: Oral bisphosphonate first-line after fragility fracture.
Denosumab requires strict 6-monthly compliance; missed doses cause rebound fractures.
Zoledronic acid IV yearly is an adherence alternative.
Teriparatide reserved for severe osteoporosis or antiresorptive failure.
explanation.pearls: After a fragility vertebral fracture with T-score less than -2.5, start weekly alendronate with calcium and vitamin D; use denosumab only when adherence to the 6-monthly injection can be assured.

A 54-year-old man presents to your practice for review 3 months after his first episode of unprovoked proximal DVT of the right femoral vein. He has completed 3 months of therapeutic apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily and is asymptomatic. He is a lifelong non-smoker with no active malignancy, no recent surgery, no travel and no hormonal therapy.

His only medication is amlodipine 5 mg for essential hypertension. He walks the dog daily and works as an office manager. His HAS-BLED score is 1 (hypertension only). He is anxious about recurrence and asks whether he should continue anticoagulation indefinitely. Baseline thrombophilia screen was not performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right calf soft, no residual swelling; no signs of chronic venous insufficiency; no chest signs
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; D-dimer today not yet measured; HAS-BLED score 1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely with annual bleeding-risk reassessment
options.rationale: Full-dose extended anticoagulation is one option but current AU guidance supports reduced-dose apixaban after 6 months in unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

options.text: Stop apixaban immediately and switch to warfarin with a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0
options.rationale: Switching to warfarin adds monitoring burden and offers no efficacy advantage over reduced-dose apixaban for extended prevention. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

options.text: Cease apixaban now and start daily aspirin 100 mg as long-term secondary prevention only
options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to a reduced-dose DOAC for extended VTE prevention and does not match the recurrence reduction achieved with apixaban 2.5 mg BD. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

options.text: Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily as extended prophylaxis with periodic review
options.rationale: After at least 6 months of full-dose therapy, extended reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily reduces recurrent VTE while limiting bleeding in low-risk patients - the AMPLIFY-EXT strategy. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

options.text: Cease all anticoagulation and use graduated compression stockings for prophylaxis only
options.rationale: Ceasing anticoagulation after 3 months in unprovoked VTE with low bleeding risk carries an annual recurrence risk near 10 percent; extended prevention is preferred. (Source: THANZ position statement: VTE)

explanation.summary: For a first unprovoked proximal DVT or PE, at least 3 months of full-dose anticoagulation is mandatory. Beyond 3 months, decisions balance annual recurrence (about 10 percent per year unprovoked, cumulative 30 percent at 5 years) against bleeding risk. In low bleeding risk (HAS-BLED under 3, no active bleeding, no recent GI bleed), extended prevention with reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily reduces recurrence with comparable bleeding to placebo (AMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN-CHOICE). Provoked VTE by a major transient risk factor completes 3 months and stops. Cancer-associated VTE continues while cancer is active.
key_points: First unprovoked VTE: minimum 3 months full-dose therapy.
Extended prevention: apixaban 2.5 mg BD or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily.
Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for extended prevention.
Provoked VTE by major transient factor: 3 months and stop.
explanation.pearls: Unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk after 6 months full-dose apixaban: step down to 2.5 mg BD extended prevention (AMPLIFY-EXT); aspirin monotherapy is inferior.

A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is reviewed after sustaining a minimal trauma right distal radius fracture after tripping on a footpath 6 weeks ago. DXA at L1-L4 shows a T-score of -3.1 and femoral neck T-score of -2.8. She has no prior fragility fractures and no known secondary causes of osteoporosis. Her serum calcium is 2.32 mmol/L, 25-OH vitamin D is 78 nmol/L, and TSH is within normal limits.

Her creatinine clearance is 62 mL/min. She has no dental problems and has not had any dental extractions or oral surgery planned. She lives independently and has no history of falls in the last 12 months apart from this one. Her calcium intake is 800 mg per day from diet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right wrist in a cast with adequate function; no other joint tenderness; no kyphosis clinically
data_table.Investigations: DXA L1-L4 T-score -3.1, femoral neck -2.8; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L; creatinine clearance 62 mL/min; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Strontium ranelate 2 g daily as first-line antiresorptive plus anabolic combined therapy
options.rationale: Strontium ranelate has been withdrawn from the Australian market due to cardiovascular safety concerns. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every 6 months as immediate first-line therapy without any bisphosphonate trial
options.rationale: Denosumab is second-line in AU or first-line only when bisphosphonates are contraindicated or not tolerated; it also carries a rebound fracture risk on cessation. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

options.text: Teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneously daily for the first 18 months of therapy
options.rationale: Teriparatide is PBS reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple minimal trauma fractures despite prior antiresorptive therapy. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

options.text: Continuous combined menopausal hormone therapy as monotherapy for osteoporosis prevention
options.rationale: MHT is not first-line for osteoporosis treatment; bone benefit ceases on stopping and there are alternative safer antiresorptive options. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly with adequate calcium and vitamin D intake maintained
options.rationale: Oral alendronate is the AU first-line agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis with minimal trauma fracture, meets PBS criteria and is well tolerated with normal creatinine clearance. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis guideline)

explanation.summary: Australian first-line treatment for postmenopausal osteoporosis with a minimal trauma fracture is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly / 150 mg monthly) with adequate calcium (1300 mg/day) and vitamin D (25-OH above 50 nmol/L). Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV yearly is an alternative for intolerance of oral therapy. Denosumab is second-line and requires an exit strategy (bisphosphonate cover) to prevent multiple vertebral fractures on discontinuation. Teriparatide is PBS reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple fractures despite antiresorptives. Assess dental health, renal function and vitamin D before initiation.
key_points: First-line: oral alendronate or risedronate + calcium + vitamin D.
Denosumab is second-line and needs an exit strategy.
Teriparatide: severe osteoporosis with failure of antiresorptive.
Strontium ranelate withdrawn in Australia.
explanation.pearls: Postmenopausal minimal trauma fracture with T-score -3.1 starts oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium 1300 mg/day and 25-OH vitamin D above 50 nmol/L; check creatinine clearance stays above 35.

stem:
An 82-year-old man is reviewed in your practice after his third fall in 6 months. All falls have been at home, without loss of consciousness, and one resulted in a Colles fracture. He lives with his wife and mobilises with a 4-wheeled walker. His medications include amitriptyline 25 mg nocte for chronic low back pain, temazepam 10 mg nocte for insomnia, oxybutynin 5 mg BD for urge incontinence, perindopril 5 mg mane, metformin 1 g BD, and rosuvastatin 20 mg nocte.

He denies angina, syncope or palpitations. Postural BP shows a drop from 138/82 lying to 108/68 standing after 3 minutes with a corresponding 12 bpm heart rate rise. Cognition is intact (MoCA 27/30). Timed Up and Go is 22 seconds. Vision is normal with current glasses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, lying blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, standing blood pressure 108/68 mmHg at 3 minutes, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented, MoCA 27/30, TUG 22 seconds; power 4+/5 lower limbs bilaterally with normal reflexes and normal joint position sense
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, TSH, B12 all within normal limits; ECG sinus rhythm at 72; HbA1c 6.9 percent

lead_in: Which medication change should be the immediate priority?

options.text: Cease temazepam and amitriptyline with a plan to review analgesic strategy separately
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines and tricyclics are the highest-risk STOPP-Frail deprescribing targets in older adults with recurrent falls; both should be tapered and stopped as the priority. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)

options.text: Reduce perindopril to 2.5 mg daily to address postural blood pressure change immediately
options.rationale: The orthostatic drop is modest and not the highest-yield falls target; benzodiazepines and TCAs have larger evidence for falls reduction on cessation. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)

options.text: Cease rosuvastatin 20 mg to remove any risk of statin-associated myopathy contributing here
options.rationale: Statin-related myopathy is uncommon and does not typically cause falls; benzodiazepines and TCAs are far higher priority for falls in the elderly. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)

options.text: Stop metformin because of the small risk of unrecognised hypoglycaemia in an older man
options.rationale: Metformin does not cause hypoglycaemia; his HbA1c is well-controlled and the risk is negligible for falls contribution. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)

options.text: Increase oxybutynin to 10 mg TDS to reduce nocturia and thus night-time toileting falls
options.rationale: Increasing an anticholinergic worsens central adverse effects and falls risk in the elderly; oxybutynin itself is a deprescribing target. (Source: RACGP Aged care - Deprescribing)

explanation.summary: Falls prevention in older adults requires multifactorial assessment: vision, hearing, gait/balance, footwear, home hazards, orthostatic blood pressure, comorbidity optimisation and medication review. STOPP-Frail identifies high-risk medications for deprescribing: benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, tricyclic antidepressants, first-generation antihistamines, anticholinergics (oxybutynin, tolterodine), opioids, typical antipsychotics, and unnecessary antihypertensives. Benzodiazepines and TCAs have the strongest evidence for falls reduction on cessation. Taper gradually to avoid withdrawal, and coordinate with non-pharmacological strategies (physiotherapy-led balance training, home OT assessment).
key_points: Multifactorial assessment underlies falls prevention.
Highest-risk medications: benzodiazepines, TCAs, anticholinergics.
Deprescribing must be gradual to avoid withdrawal.
Combine with balance training and home OT review.
explanation.pearls: In a falling older adult on both temazepam and amitriptyline, plan a coordinated taper and cessation of both as the first-line intervention; benzodiazepines and TCAs are the top STOPP-Frail falls targets.

A 32-year-old man is diagnosed with HIV after a routine STI screen prompted by high-risk sexual practices. His baseline CD4 count is 480 cells/microlitre, HIV RNA viral load is 82,000 copies/mL, and HLA-B*5701 is negative. Confirmatory Western blot is positive. He has no opportunistic infections and is otherwise well. Baseline biochemistry, hepatitis serology (HBV surface antigen negative, immune to HAV, HCV negative) and syphilis serology are unremarkable.

He is highly motivated for treatment and asks about starting antiretroviral therapy at his next visit. He works full-time in hospitality and has good private health insurance. He has no active psychiatric symptoms and is not injecting drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no lymphadenopathy; no oral candida; no rashes; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: CD4 480 cells/microlitre; HIV RNA 82,000 copies/mL; HLA-B*5701 negative; HBsAg negative; HAV IgG positive; HCV negative; creatinine 78 micromol/L; ALT 26 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antiretroviral plan?

options.text: Defer therapy until CD4 falls below 350 cells/microlitre before commencing combination therapy
options.rationale: Deferring ART is superseded; ART is recommended for all HIV-positive adults regardless of CD4 count in Australia. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

options.text: Commence a single-tablet regimen of bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide within days
options.rationale: Rapid start of a preferred integrase-inhibitor based single-tablet regimen (bictegravir/emtricitabine/TAF) is standard in Australia once baseline results permit safe initiation. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

options.text: Start efavirenz-based combination therapy at initial diagnosis because of cost advantage
options.rationale: Efavirenz has neuropsychiatric side effects and is no longer first-line; integrase inhibitor based regimens (bictegravir, dolutegravir) are preferred. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

options.text: Commence dolutegravir monotherapy while awaiting resistance testing and full staging results
options.rationale: Monotherapy is inadequate; the AU standard remains a three-drug regimen or a validated two-drug regimen with NRTI backbone, not monotherapy. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

options.text: Prescribe abacavir plus lamivudine plus dolutegravir triple therapy without HLA typing
options.rationale: Abacavir requires HLA-B*5701 negative status before initiation to avoid hypersensitivity syndrome; typing must be done before starting. (Source: ASHM Australian Consensus HIV guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australian HIV guidance (ASHM) recommends antiretroviral therapy for all people living with HIV regardless of CD4 count, with rapid start (ideally within 7 days of diagnosis) once baseline safety labs and hepatitis screening are back. Preferred first-line regimens are single-tablet integrase inhibitor based combinations: bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (BIC/FTC/TAF) or dolutegravir with lamivudine (2-drug) or dolutegravir with tenofovir/emtricitabine (3-drug). Abacavir-based regimens require HLA-B*5701 negative status. Undetectable viral load equals untransmittable (U equals U) and is the treatment goal. Baseline resistance testing is performed but does not delay treatment initiation.
key_points: ART is recommended for all PLHIV regardless of CD4.
Rapid start ideally within 7 days of diagnosis.
First-line: integrase inhibitor STR (BIC/FTC/TAF).
Abacavir requires HLA-B*5701 negative.
explanation.pearls: New HIV diagnosis with hepatitis B and HLA-B*5701 negative: start BIC/FTC/TAF single tablet within days, do not wait for CD4 threshold or full resistance report before initiation.

A 28-year-old woman from Vietnam has been in Australia for 12 months. She is a nurse and completed pre-employment screening. Her interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) returned positive. She has no cough, night sweats, weight loss or fevers. Chest X-ray is clear. She has no history of BCG vaccination that she can recall.

She is HIV negative and not immunosuppressed. She is on the combined oral contraceptive pill. LFTs are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of liver disease and drinks no alcohol. She is not pregnant and does not plan to conceive in the next year. She is highly motivated to complete treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; no lymphadenopathy; chest clear on auscultation; abdomen soft with no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus positive; chest X-ray clear; HIV negative; ALT 22 U/L (<40); ALT normal; bilirubin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment regimen?

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg daily monotherapy for 4 months without concurrent isoniazid cover
options.rationale: Rifampicin monotherapy for 4 months (4R) is an alternative but interacts strongly with combined oral contraceptives - counselling and additional contraception are required; 3HP is preferred here. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus rifampicin 600 mg daily for 12 months orally at home
options.rationale: 12 months of dual therapy exceeds evidence-based durations for latent TB; short-course regimens are preferred. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus rifapentine weekly for 12 weeks under directly observed therapy
options.rationale: Short-course rifapentine plus isoniazid for 12 weeks (3HP) is a preferred CDNA/NTAC regimen for latent TB in adults with good adherence, matching daily 9-month isoniazid for efficacy at lower duration. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)

options.text: Directly observed active TB treatment with 4 drugs regardless of chest X-ray result
options.rationale: Active TB treatment is not indicated in latent infection; asymptomatic with clear CXR excludes active disease. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)

options.text: Observation with annual QuantiFERON testing and no pharmacotherapy for the latent infection
options.rationale: Untreated latent TB in a healthcare worker carries a 5 to 10 percent lifetime reactivation risk; treatment is indicated per CDNA/NTAC. (Source: CDNA/NTAC latent TB guidance)

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection (positive IGRA or TST without symptoms, signs or radiographic evidence of active disease) is treated in adults at increased risk of reactivation (healthcare workers, HIV, TNF inhibitor users, close contacts). Preferred CDNA/NTAC regimens are: isoniazid + rifapentine weekly for 12 doses (3HP), isoniazid daily for 6 or 9 months (6H or 9H), rifampicin daily for 4 months (4R), or isoniazid + rifampicin for 3 or 4 months (3HR/4HR). 3HP has the best completion rates. Rifamycin interactions with combined oral contraception are important - counsel on additional contraception.
key_points: 3HP (isoniazid + rifapentine 12 weeks) is preferred for completion.
6H or 9H isoniazid daily are alternatives.
Rifampicin interacts with oral contraceptives.
Baseline and monitoring LFTs required.
explanation.pearls: Positive IGRA healthcare worker with clear chest X-ray and normal LFTs: 3HP (weekly isoniazid + rifapentine for 12 doses under directly observed therapy) is the preferred short-course regimen.
