A 42-year-old woman presents to your practice with 10 weeks of symmetric painful swelling of the MCP and PIP joints of both hands, morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes, and fatigue. She has no extra-articular symptoms. Rheumatoid factor is 68 IU/mL (<20), anti-CCP is 108 U/mL (<20), CRP is 48 mg/L, and ESR is 62 mm/hr. Hand X-rays are unremarkable for erosions but show soft tissue swelling around the MCPs.

She has completed her family and is not breastfeeding. She drinks no alcohol. LFTs and renal function are within normal limits. She is up to date with cervical screening. Chest X-ray is clear. Rheumatology outpatient wait time is 6 weeks. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symmetric synovitis of MCP 2-4 and PIP 2-4 bilaterally with soft swelling; power maintained; no rheumatoid nodules
data_table.Investigations: Rheumatoid factor 68 IU/mL; anti-CCP 108 U/mL; CRP 48 mg/L; ESR 62 mm/hr; ALT 22 U/L; creatinine 68 micromol/L; hand X-rays: soft tissue swelling only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Refer to rheumatology in 6 weeks and give no medical management pending specialist input
options.rationale: Six-week deferral risks irreversible joint damage; the window-of-opportunity concept supports DMARD start within 3 months. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)

options.text: Prescribe oral prednisolone 20 mg daily and defer any DMARD selection to specialist review
options.rationale: Steroid monotherapy without DMARD cover allows joint damage to progress; DMARD should not be delayed by weeks awaiting specialist review. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)

options.text: Prescribe naproxen 500 mg twice daily and celecoxib 200 mg for symptom control only
options.rationale: NSAIDs treat symptoms but do not prevent erosive joint damage; disease-modifying therapy is required in early RA. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)

options.text: Commence oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly and urgent rheumatology referral
options.rationale: Early RA benefits from DMARD initiation within 3 months of symptom onset; methotrexate is the anchor drug and can be started while awaiting specialist review per RACGP/ARA guidance. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)

options.text: Immediate high-dose infliximab infusion in the community without prior methotrexate trial
options.rationale: Biologic DMARDs are reserved for failure of conventional synthetic DMARDs and require rheumatologist-led initiation with screening. (Source: ARA rheumatoid arthritis guideline)

explanation.summary: Early rheumatoid arthritis (symptom duration under 6 months, seropositive with anti-CCP, elevated inflammatory markers, symmetric small joint involvement) benefits from disease-modifying therapy within 3 months of onset - the window of opportunity. Methotrexate is the AU/international anchor drug: start 10-15 mg weekly PO with folic acid 5 mg weekly. Bridging low-dose prednisolone (10-15 mg tapered over 6-8 weeks) controls symptoms while methotrexate takes effect. Baseline FBC, LFTs, renal function, hepatitis B and C screening, and chest X-ray are required before start. Biologic DMARDs (TNF inhibitors, JAK inhibitors) are second-line after csDMARD failure.
key_points: Window of opportunity: DMARD within 3 months of onset.
Methotrexate 10-15 mg weekly + folic acid is anchor therapy.
Bridging prednisolone taper covers slow methotrexate onset.
Baseline hepatitis, TB and chest X-ray screening before start.
explanation.pearls: Early seropositive symmetric small joint synovitis with anti-CCP 108 and CRP 48 warrants methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid and urgent rheumatology referral; do not wait 6 weeks for the specialist appointment.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman presents to your practice with 6 migraine episodes per month over the past 4 months. Each episode lasts 24 hours, causes her to miss work, and responds partially to oral sumatriptan 50 mg. She has no aura. Her past medical history includes moderate persistent asthma well-controlled on Symbicort maintenance and reliever. She has no depression, no cardiac history, and no pregnancy plans over the next 12 months.

Her only regular medications are Symbicort and paracetamol as needed. She does not use oral contraception. She has trialled magnesium 400 mg daily for 3 months without benefit. She has identified triggers of poor sleep and skipping meals which she is addressing with sleep hygiene and structured eating.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, oriented; cranial nerve exam within normal limits; no focal neurology; fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: FBC, TSH, UEC within normal limits; no imaging indicated by red flag review

lead_in: What is the most appropriate migraine prophylaxis to commence?

options.text: Propranolol 40 mg twice daily titrated to 80 mg twice daily over 4 weeks as needed
options.rationale: Propranolol is usually first-line migraine prophylaxis, but is relatively contraindicated in moderate persistent asthma and a non-cardioselective beta-blocker may worsen bronchospasm. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

options.text: Continue current sumatriptan and add regular paracetamol daily as prophylaxis at home
options.rationale: Regular daily paracetamol risks medication overuse headache and is not effective prophylaxis; prophylactic therapy needs a targeted evidence-based agent. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

options.text: Sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1500 mg total daily dose over 4 weeks
options.rationale: Valproate is effective for migraine prophylaxis but is contraindicated in women of childbearing age unless pregnancy prevention criteria are strictly met due to teratogenicity risk. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

options.text: Verapamil 80 mg three times daily as prophylaxis with cardiac ECG at baseline before start
options.rationale: Verapamil is used for cluster headache prophylaxis rather than migraine; it lacks the evidence base of TCAs, beta-blockers or topiramate for migraine. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

options.text: Amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated up to 25 to 50 mg nocte over 4 to 6 weeks as tolerated
options.rationale: In a patient where beta-blocker is unsuitable (moderate persistent asthma), amitriptyline is a preferred first-line migraine prophylactic per Australian eTG. (Source: Australian eTG: Neurology - Migraine)

explanation.summary: Migraine prophylaxis is indicated for 4 or more monthly migraine days, or fewer episodes that significantly impair function. Australian eTG first-line agents are propranolol (first-line if no contraindication), amitriptyline (preferred if asthma, comorbid tension headache or insomnia), topiramate, sodium valproate (contraindicated in women of childbearing age without strict pregnancy prevention), pizotifen and candesartan. Newer CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) are PBS-listed for refractory chronic migraine after failure of 3 prior classes. Trial each agent for 8-12 weeks at target dose before considering failure.
key_points: Prophylaxis threshold: 4+ migraine days per month or significant impairment.
Propranolol is first-line unless asthma, brady, hypotension.
Amitriptyline is preferred with asthma or insomnia comorbidity.
Valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing age.
explanation.pearls: Frequent migraine in an asthmatic woman: skip propranolol, choose amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated to 25-50 mg; trial for 8-12 weeks before deeming ineffective.

sources.label: Australian Headache Society: Migraine management position statement

stem:
A 42-year-old woman presents to your practice with 12 months of progressive central weight gain (9 kg), easy bruising on her arms with minimal trauma, new-onset hypertension requiring a second agent, oligomenorrhoea and mood lability. Her mother had breast cancer at 62. She has striae 8 mm wide across her abdomen and flanks that are purple. She takes amlodipine 5 mg and irbesartan 150 mg for blood pressure.

She has no exogenous glucocorticoid use, including no inhaled or intra-articular steroids. She drinks 1 to 2 standard drinks per week and does not shift-work. Random morning cortisol taken by another practitioner was 480 nmol/L. Fasting glucose is 6.8 mmol/L, and HbA1c is 6.5 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg on two agents, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity with dorsocervical fat pad; wide purple striae on abdomen and flanks; proximal muscle weakness; easy bruising on arms
data_table.Investigations: Random morning cortisol 480 nmol/L; fasting glucose 6.8 mmol/L; HbA1c 6.5 percent; potassium 3.6 mmol/L; no exogenous steroid use

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line screening investigation?

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with morning cortisol at 08:00 the next day
options.rationale: 1 mg overnight DST is a preferred Endocrine Society and Australian first-line screen for suspected Cushing syndrome; a morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L suggests failure of suppression and warrants further investigation. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)

options.text: Plasma ACTH measurement in a single early morning sample as the initial screening test
options.rationale: ACTH is used to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing after diagnosis is established, not as a screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)

options.text: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling to localise the source of ACTH secretion definitively
options.rationale: IPSS is a highly specialised test for distinguishing pituitary from ectopic ACTH after Cushing is confirmed and ACTH-dependent aetiology established. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)

options.text: Random single serum cortisol interpreted against a fixed cut-off value of 500 nanomole/L
options.rationale: Random cortisol is unreliable due to diurnal variation; screening uses 1 mg DST, 24 hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)

options.text: CT of the adrenal glands and pituitary MRI before any biochemical confirmation is undertaken
options.rationale: Imaging before biochemistry generates incidentaloma noise (adrenal nodules are common); biochemical confirmation must come first. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing guideline)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome is investigated stepwise: confirm hypercortisolism biochemically before any imaging or localisation. First-line screening tests (any two positive out of three, or one strongly positive with high clinical suspicion) are 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression (cortisol under 50 nmol/L excludes), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (2-3 collections), and late-night salivary cortisol (loss of diurnal rhythm). Once confirmed, plasma ACTH distinguishes ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) aetiology, then imaging directs pituitary vs ectopic vs adrenal disease. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is reserved for ACTH-dependent cases with equivocal pituitary MRI.
key_points: Confirm hypercortisolism before any imaging.
1 mg DST, 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary are screens.
ACTH after confirmation distinguishes dependent from independent.
IPSS for equivocal ACTH-dependent pituitary MRI.
explanation.pearls: Suspected Cushing: start with 1 mg overnight DST and 08:00 cortisol; only after confirmed hypercortisolism measure ACTH and image.

stem:
A 68-year-old male ex-smoker (30 pack-years, quit 8 years ago) presents to your respiratory outpatient clinic with 12 months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. He has bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing. His FVC is 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, and DLCO is 42 percent predicted.

He has no rash, joint symptoms, or Raynaud's phenomenon. Autoimmune serology (ANA, ENA, anti-CCP, RF, MPO, PR3) is negative. He has never worked in mining, construction or with asbestos. HRCT chest today shows peripheral and basal reticulation with honeycombing 5 mm subpleural cysts and traction bronchiectasis, with no ground glass and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bibasal fine end-inspiratory crackles; finger clubbing; no rash; no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: FVC 68 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, DLCO 42 percent predicted; autoimmune serology negative; HRCT: definite UIP pattern with honeycombing

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Empirical high-dose prednisolone 60 mg daily for 6 weeks to arrest disease progression
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy does not benefit IPF and may harm; antifibrotic therapy is the standard. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: Refer to a specialist ILD multidisciplinary team for antifibrotic therapy consideration
options.rationale: A definite UIP pattern on HRCT in a clinical context of IPF meets AU criteria to refer for antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) via a specialist ILD service. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: Surgical lung biopsy from the right lower lobe to obtain definitive tissue diagnosis first
options.rationale: Definite UIP pattern on HRCT in the appropriate clinical context does not require surgical biopsy per current AU guidance; biopsy is reserved for probable or indeterminate UIP. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: N-acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily as antioxidant monotherapy for slow progression
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine monotherapy in IPF was not superior to placebo (PANTHER-IPF) and is not recommended. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

options.text: Reassurance and 12-month observation with repeat HRCT to confirm progression before treatment
options.rationale: IPF is progressive; deferring antifibrotic therapy allows irreversible loss of function which cannot be recovered. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

explanation.summary: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive fibrotic interstitial lung disease diagnosed by an ILD multidisciplinary team using HRCT and clinical assessment. Definite UIP pattern on HRCT (basal and peripheral reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis, no atypical features) in an appropriate clinical context does not require surgical lung biopsy. Antifibrotic therapy (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slows FVC decline and is PBS-listed for FVC 50-80 percent predicted and DLCO 30-79 percent predicted. Non-pharmacological care includes pulmonary rehabilitation, smoking cessation, oxygen for hypoxaemia, vaccinations, and early lung transplant referral for suitable candidates.
key_points: Definite HRCT UIP + clinical context = IPF diagnosis without biopsy.
Antifibrotics (pirfenidone or nintedanib) slow FVC decline.
PBS criteria: FVC 50-80 and DLCO 30-79 predicted.
Steroids and NAC monotherapy not indicated.
explanation.pearls: Definite UIP on HRCT with FVC 68 and DLCO 42 in a clinical IPF phenotype: refer to ILD MDT for pirfenidone or nintedanib; do not use steroids or NAC as primary therapy.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia IPF position statement

stem:
A 66-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 24 hours of fever, productive cough, pleuritic left-sided chest pain and confusion. He usually lives independently and manages his own affairs but today he cannot recall the day of the week. He has stage 3 CKD (baseline creatinine 150 micromol/L) and hypertension.

On examination he has bronchial breathing at the left lower zone and dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation. SMART-COP score is 5. His lactate is 3.4 mmol/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 240 mg/L. Blood cultures have been taken. He is not immunosuppressed and has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 89 percent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: New confusion (AMT 6/10); bronchial breathing left lower zone with dullness to percussion; peripheries cool
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 240 mg/L; lactate 3.4 mmol/L; creatinine 220 micromol/L; blood cultures pending; CXR left lower lobe consolidation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic combination?

options.text: IV amoxicillin 1 g plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily now
options.rationale: For severe CAP with SMART-COP 5 and organ dysfunction, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is the Australian eTG regimen rather than amoxicillin plus gentamicin. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g plus oral doxycycline 100 mg for community treatment at home tonight
options.rationale: SMART-COP 5 mandates inpatient IV therapy with ICU review; oral outpatient treatment is unsafe. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus IV azithromycin 500 mg then IV fluid resuscitation and reassessment
options.rationale: SMART-COP 5 defines severe CAP requiring ICU-capable care; the Australian eTG severe CAP regimen is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (or moxifloxacin monotherapy if beta-lactam allergy). (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: IV piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g plus IV vancomycin as broad-spectrum first-line therapy
options.rationale: Broad Gram negative and MRSA cover is not first-line for community-acquired pneumonia; ceftriaxone plus azithromycin covers typical and atypical pathogens. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

options.text: IV meropenem 1 g monotherapy every 8 hours for empirical broad-spectrum antimicrobial cover
options.rationale: Meropenem is inappropriate first-line for CAP; it drives selection pressure for resistance and is reserved for hospital-acquired or resistant infection. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

explanation.summary: Australian severity-stratified community-acquired pneumonia (SMART-COP: Systolic BP under 90, Multilobar CXR, Albumin under 35, Respiratory rate raised, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygenation low, pH under 7.35) directs treatment intensity. SMART-COP 5 or above signals severe disease requiring ICU-capable care and dual IV antibiotic therapy: ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (or benzylpenicillin) plus IV azithromycin 500 mg daily to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical pathogens (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia). Moxifloxacin monotherapy is an alternative for beta-lactam allergy. Sepsis hour-1 bundle includes lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, IV antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor if not fluid-responsive.
key_points: SMART-COP 5+ triggers severe CAP pathway.
Severe CAP: IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin.
Hour-1 sepsis bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluid.
Moxifloxacin monotherapy for severe beta-lactam allergy.
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP 5 with lactate 3.4 mandates IV ceftriaxone 1 g plus IV azithromycin 500 mg within the sepsis hour; cultures first, then antibiotics, then 30 mL/kg crystalloid.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Community acquired pneumonia

stem:
A 34-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 24 hours of fever, right flank pain, dysuria and urinary frequency. She has vomited once but tolerates oral fluids and food now. She has no relevant past medical history and takes no regular medications. She is not pregnant (recent period 10 days ago, contraception with the LNG-IUS in situ).

On examination she has right renal angle tenderness and mild suprapubic tenderness without peritonism. Urinalysis shows blood, leucocytes and nitrites; MSU sent. She has social supports at home and can attend for reassessment at 48 hours if needed. She is not systemically septic - HR 92, BP 122/76, RR 18, SpO2 99, temperature 38.4.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; abdomen soft with right renal angle tenderness and mild suprapubic tenderness; no peritonism; genitalia unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: blood, leucocytes and nitrites; MSU sent; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 3 days at home with a review at 48 hours in clinic
options.rationale: Trimethoprim short course treats uncomplicated cystitis not pyelonephritis; pyelonephritis requires an oral fluoroquinolone or cefalexin equivalent for 10 to 14 days. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg four times daily for 7 days from your general practice today
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentrations for pyelonephritis and is restricted to cystitis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Admit for IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg and IV ampicillin every 6 hours until afebrile 48 hours
options.rationale: IV therapy is reserved for severe sepsis, pregnancy, inability to tolerate oral, or failure of oral therapy; she is systemically well and tolerating fluids. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days with clinic review at 48 hours from now
options.rationale: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis in a systemically well adult who tolerates oral intake is managed as an outpatient with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days per Australian eTG. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days as first-line empirical antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Amoxicillin resistance rates in E coli exceed 50 percent and empirical amoxicillin monotherapy is inadequate for pyelonephritis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant adult who is systemically well and can tolerate oral fluids is managed as an outpatient per Australian eTG. First-line oral therapy is ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (double strength) BD for 14 days if fluoroquinolone contraindicated. Cefalexin 500 mg QID for 14 days is an alternative. Admission for IV therapy is required for severe sepsis, pregnancy, uncontrolled vomiting, urinary tract obstruction (needs urgent drainage), or failure of oral therapy at 48 hours. Urine culture guides definitive therapy; imaging (renal ultrasound or CT) is reserved for recurrent infection, poor response or suspected obstruction.
key_points: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis: oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days.
Admission for IV: severe sepsis, pregnancy, vomiting, obstruction.
Trimethoprim short course is for cystitis only.
Nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis.
explanation.pearls: Well non-pregnant adult with pyelonephritis who tolerates oral fluids: outpatient ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 7 days with 48 hour review; admit if severe sepsis, pregnancy or ongoing vomiting.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Urinary tract infection
Cochrane 2010: Antibiotic regimens for acute pyelonephritis

stem:
A 74-year-old woman on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve replacement (target INR 2.5 to 3.5) presents to the emergency department with a 4-hour history of sudden severe headache and left-sided weakness. Her CT brain shows a right-sided intracerebral haemorrhage in the basal ganglia measuring 35 mm with mild midline shift. Her INR on arrival is 3.8.

She is drowsy but rousable, moving all four limbs with 3/5 power on the left and 5/5 on the right. She was last stable INR 3 weeks ago at 2.6. Her regular medications also include perindopril, amlodipine and atorvastatin. She has no known drug allergies. She weighs 68 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 176/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3V4M6); left hemiparesis 3/5; right side 5/5; pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: INR 3.8; APTT 42 sec; platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-450); creatinine 92 micromol/L; CT brain: 35 mm right basal ganglia ICH with mild midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII (rFVIIa) as a single bolus dose given intravenously today
options.rationale: rFVIIa is not routinely used for warfarin reversal; prothrombinex provides balanced factor replacement and is the AU standard. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg oral only and observe INR trend for the next 6 hours prior to reassessment
options.rationale: Oral vitamin K is too slow (24 to 48 hours to lower INR) for a life-threatening ICH; IV route and factor replacement are required. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg IV alone as reversal without any additional intervention
options.rationale: FFP alone requires large volumes and delivers unpredictable factor levels; prothrombinex is preferred and provides faster INR correction. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)

options.text: Idarucizumab 5 g IV as immediate warfarin reversal in the emergency department resuscitation
options.rationale: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; there is no role in warfarin-associated bleeding. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)

options.text: Vitamin K 10 mg IV plus prothrombinex 50 units/kg IV given as soon as they can be prepared
options.rationale: Major bleeding on warfarin (any life-threatening or intracranial bleed) requires immediate reversal with IV vitamin K plus prothrombinex per Australian THANZ/AHRTC guidance; FFP alone is inadequate. (Source: THANZ Warfarin reversal consensus)

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding, including any intracranial haemorrhage or life-threatening bleed at any INR, requires immediate reversal per Australian THANZ consensus. The standard combination is IV vitamin K 10 mg (works over 6-24 hours) plus prothrombinex 25-50 units/kg (works within minutes to hours). Vitamin K provides sustained reversal by allowing hepatic synthesis of clotting factors; prothrombinex provides immediate factor II, VII, IX, X replacement. FFP is used only if prothrombinex is unavailable, at 15 mL/kg. Recheck INR at 30 minutes and repeat prothrombinex if INR remains above 1.5. Blood pressure control (systolic under 140) reduces haematoma expansion in ICH.
key_points: Warfarin major bleed: IV vitamin K + prothrombinex.
Vitamin K sustains reversal; prothrombinex is immediate.
FFP is a backup only when prothrombinex unavailable.
Idarucizumab is for dabigatran, andexanet for FXa inhibitors.
explanation.pearls: Warfarin ICH with INR 3.8: IV vitamin K 10 mg + prothrombinex 50 units/kg immediately; check INR at 30 min and target under 1.5; drop systolic BP to under 140 to limit expansion.

subtopic_detail: HIV opportunistic infection prophylaxis by CD4 count
stem:
A 38-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV attends your general practice for co-management with the ID physician. His baseline bloods show HIV viral load 240000 copies/mL, CD4 count 140 cells/microL, and toxoplasma IgG negative. He is asymptomatic and antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine) is being started this week. His BMI is 24 kg/m2, blood pressure is normal.

He has no allergies. His previous investigations show normal renal function, LFTs and glucose. Latent tuberculosis screening with QFT-Plus is pending and CXR was clear. He is up to date with all vaccinations and has already received the annual influenza vaccine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy; no oral candidiasis; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: HIV VL 240000 copies/mL; CD4 140 cells/microL; toxoplasma IgG negative; QFT-Plus pending; CXR clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylaxis regimen to commence now?

options.text: Fluconazole 200 mg orally daily for oesophageal candida and cryptococcal prophylaxis today
options.rationale: Primary antifungal prophylaxis is not routine in Australian HIV care regardless of CD4 count at this level. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

options.text: Ganciclovir 1 g orally three times daily for CMV retinitis prophylaxis regardless of CMV status
options.rationale: CMV prophylaxis is not recommended primarily; treatment is initiated only if end-organ disease is diagnosed. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

options.text: Dapsone 100 mg orally daily plus pyrimethamine-folinic acid today as combined regimen
options.rationale: Dapsone is an alternative to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in sulfa allergy; combined pyrimethamine-folinic acid is for toxoplasmosis in seropositive patients only. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally daily as sole opportunistic infection prophylaxis for now
options.rationale: ASHM guidance starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) at CD4 below 200 for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis; toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is not required as IgG is negative. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

options.text: Azithromycin 1200 mg orally weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis today
options.rationale: MAC prophylaxis is only added when CD4 falls below 50 in Australian guidance and is being de-emphasised with early ART. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV Consensus)

explanation.summary: Australian HIV opportunistic infection prophylaxis follows CD4-based thresholds. Below 200 cells/microL: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily (or three times weekly) for Pneumocystis pneumonia; dapsone 100 mg daily is an alternative in sulfa allergy. Below 100 cells/microL with positive toxoplasma IgG: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole also covers toxoplasmosis (dapsone plus pyrimethamine-folinic acid in sulfa allergy). Below 50 cells/microL: MAC prophylaxis with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly, though it is being de-emphasised as early ART restores immunity rapidly. Prophylaxis is stopped once CD4 rises above 200 for at least 3 months on sustained virological suppression.
key_points: PCP prophylaxis starts at CD4 below 200 with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Toxoplasma cover comes with the same drug when IgG is positive.
MAC prophylaxis is reserved for CD4 below 50 and is being de-emphasised.
Stop prophylaxis when CD4 above 200 for 3 months on suppressive ART.
explanation.pearls: At CD4 140 with negative toxoplasma IgG, start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg daily for Pneumocystis pneumonia prophylaxis; add MAC prophylaxis only if CD4 falls below 50.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - HIV opportunistic infections

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis pharmacological threshold from DXA and FRAX
stem:
A 66-year-old woman presents to your general practice for a routine health check. She is postmenopausal since age 52 and has never used menopausal hormone therapy. Her mother had a hip fracture at age 78. She takes calcium 500 mg daily and vitamin D 1000 IU daily. She has never had a fragility fracture herself, but she stumbled twice in the last year without injury.

Her BMI is 24 kg/m2, blood pressure normal, and she does not smoke or drink alcohol. Recent DXA scan reports lumbar spine T-score of -2.6, femoral neck T-score of -2.7 and total hip T-score of -2.4. Her calculated 10-year FRAX for major osteoporotic fracture is 22 percent and 10-year hip fracture risk is 5.2 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No kyphosis; no bony tenderness; mobility unaided; no gait abnormality
data_table.Investigations: DXA lumbar spine T -2.6; femoral neck T -2.7; total hip T -2.4; 10-year FRAX major osteoporotic 22 percent; hip 5.2 percent; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60); vitamin D 78 nmol/L (>=50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological plan?

options.text: Repeat DXA scan in 2 years without any change to current calcium and vitamin D regimen
options.rationale: A T-score of -2.5 or lower meets the diagnostic criterion for osteoporosis; observation without pharmacotherapy is undertreatment. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Start teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneous daily as first-line treatment straightaway
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis with T-score below -3.0 and prior fracture on bisphosphonate; bisphosphonate is first-line here. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Commence tibolone 2.5 mg daily for combined osteoporosis and vasomotor symptom management
options.rationale: Tibolone is not first-line osteoporosis therapy for a 66 year old without vasomotor symptoms; bisphosphonate is preferred. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Start strontium ranelate 2 g daily instead of a bisphosphonate for equivalent fracture prevention
options.rationale: Strontium ranelate carries cardiovascular risk and is now rarely used; bisphosphonates are the standard of care. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

options.text: Commence oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with continued calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: RACGP osteoporosis guidelines recommend pharmacotherapy for T-score at or below -2.5 or any minimal trauma fracture; alendronate weekly is the first-line bisphosphonate. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

explanation.summary: The RACGP osteoporosis guideline uses DXA T-score, minimal trauma fracture history and 10-year absolute fracture risk (FRAX or Garvan) to decide pharmacotherapy. Pharmacotherapy is indicated for T-score at or below -2.5, or any minimal trauma vertebral fracture, or 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk of 20 percent or more with any low bone density, or a hip fracture 3 percent or more. First-line agents are oral alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly. IV zoledronic acid 5 mg annually is an alternative for oral intolerance. Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous 6 monthly is second-line, and abrupt cessation risks rebound vertebral fracture, so it needs a bisphosphonate follow-on if discontinued.
key_points: Pharmacotherapy is indicated for T-score at or below -2.5 or any minimal trauma vertebral fracture.
First-line is oral alendronate or risedronate weekly.
IV zoledronic acid annually is an alternative for oral intolerance.
Denosumab needs bisphosphonate follow-on if stopped to avoid rebound fracture.
explanation.pearls: A T-score of -2.5 or lower on DXA meets the RACGP threshold for pharmacotherapy; start alendronate 70 mg weekly with continued calcium and vitamin D.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis Prevention Diagnosis and Management

stem:
A 54-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 6 hour severe frontal headache, blurred vision, and one episode of vomiting. She has a background of hypertension on ramipril 10 mg daily but has been non-adherent for 3 weeks. She does not smoke. On arrival her BP is 218/128 mmHg confirmed on repeat measurement, pulse 96/min sinus. Neurological examination shows no focal deficit but grade 3 hypertensive retinopathy with flame haemorrhages bilaterally on fundoscopy.

Her creatinine is 138 micromol/L (compared to 88 baseline 6 months ago), urinalysis shows 2+ protein and no red cells, troponin is negative and ECG shows LV hypertrophy without ST changes. CT brain is unremarkable and demonstrates no haemorrhage. She has no chest pain and no aortic dissection features.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 218/128 mmHg (repeated), respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 15; no focal neurology; grade 3 retinopathy with flame haemorrhages; chest clear; no cardiac murmur
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 138 micromol/L (baseline 88); urinalysis 2+ protein; troponin negative; ECG LVH; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antihypertensive?

options.text: IV labetalol 20 mg bolus with a target BP reduction of 25 percent over the first hour then further gradual reduction
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance treats hypertensive emergency with 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour using IV labetalol or GTN; overly aggressive reduction risks watershed cerebral ischaemia. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

options.text: IV nitroprusside starting at 3 microgram/kg/min targeting BP of 120/80 within 30 minutes
options.rationale: Rapid BP normalisation risks cerebral, coronary and renal hypoperfusion; the target is 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 20 mg immediate-release for rapid uncontrolled reduction as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine causes uncontrolled precipitous BP drops and is not recommended in hypertensive emergency. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

options.text: Resume oral ramipril 10 mg once daily with observation over 4 hours as sole intervention
options.rationale: Oral ramipril is too slow-acting for hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage; IV therapy is required for controlled reduction. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

options.text: IV thiazide diuretic bolus of furosemide 40 mg alone as monotherapy for acute BP control
options.rationale: Furosemide addresses volume overload and pulmonary oedema but is not first-line for hypertensive emergency without those features. (Source: Australian eTG: Cardiovascular - Hypertensive emergency)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency requires end-organ damage (encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, acute kidney injury, aortic dissection, retinopathy grade 3-4) alongside severely elevated BP (generally above 180/120). Treatment uses IV antihypertensive therapy to reduce mean arterial pressure by approximately 25 percent over the first hour, then to 160/100-110 over the next 2 to 6 hours, then to normal over 24 to 48 hours. First-line agents include IV labetalol, IV GTN (if myocardial ischaemia or pulmonary oedema), IV hydralazine, or IV clevidipine. Nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases due to cyanide toxicity risk. Aortic dissection requires more rapid BP and heart rate control (SBP below 120, HR below 60) with esmolol plus GTN or nitroprusside.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency needs end-organ damage plus severe BP.
Target 25 percent MAP reduction in the first hour.
First-line agents: IV labetalol, IV GTN, IV hydralazine or IV clevidipine.
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated due to uncontrolled drops.
explanation.pearls: Reduce MAP by no more than 25 percent in the first hour in hypertensive emergency with IV labetalol or GTN; sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated.

sources.label: NHMRC Guide to management of hypertension

stem:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin presents to the emergency department with severe pain and swelling of his right leg for 24 hours. The pain seems disproportionate to the visible cellulitis on his shin. He described the affected area as feeling numb over the past 2 hours. He has crepitus on palpation and a small area of dusky discolouration. He has no recent trauma but reports a small unnoticed skin abrasion 3 days ago.

On examination he looks unwell, is confused (GCS 14), and has marked tenderness over the shin extending along the fascial planes. Blood tests: WCC 22 x10^9/L, Hb 128 g/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 148 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, CRP 240 mg/L. Lactate 3.2 mmol/L. He is fluid-responsive but tachycardic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg (improved to 106 after 1 L crystalloid), respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right shin with pain out of proportion, dusky discolouration, crepitus on palpation, sensory reduction over affected area, no dorsalis pedis pulse loss
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L; Hb 128 g/L; Na 132 mmol/L; Cr 148 micromol/L (baseline 88); glucose 16 mmol/L; CRP 240 mg/L; lactate 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with observation in the short stay unit for 12 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis; parenteral broad-spectrum cover and urgent surgery are required. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Urgent surgical review for operative debridement with concurrent IV meropenem, vancomycin and clindamycin
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, crepitus, systemic sepsis and LRINEC-score risk factors in a diabetic mandates urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g four times daily alone with elevation and outpatient review in 24 hours
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis needs both broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic and toxin-suppression cover plus urgent surgical debridement; monotherapy misses gram-negative and anaerobic pathogens. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: MRI of the affected leg first to confirm the diagnosis before considering any surgery
options.rationale: MRI delays definitive surgery and should not precede operative exploration when the clinical suspicion is strong; the diagnosis is clinical or surgical. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the primary intervention before surgery or antibiotics
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen may be adjunctive later but is never a substitute for surgical debridement and antibiotics in the acute presentation. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Necrotising fasciitis)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency where diagnosis rests on clinical signs (pain out of proportion, rapid progression, crepitus, dusky skin, sensory changes over the affected area, systemic sepsis) supplemented by the Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis (LRINEC) score: CRP, WCC, Hb, sodium, creatinine, glucose. A score of 6 or more raises suspicion; a score of 8 or more is high probability. However, LRINEC does not replace clinical judgement and imaging must not delay surgery when suspicion is high. Empirical antibiotics are broad-spectrum: piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (for toxin suppression). Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive intervention; delay increases mortality substantially.
key_points: Necrotising fasciitis diagnosis is largely clinical; imaging should not delay surgery.
LRINEC score aids risk stratification but does not replace clinical judgement.
Empirical antibiotics: meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
Urgent surgical debridement is the definitive intervention.
explanation.pearls: In suspected necrotising fasciitis, pain out of proportion plus crepitus plus sepsis in a diabetic mandates immediate surgical review and IV meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin before any imaging.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency on maintenance hydrocortisone 20 mg mane and 10 mg mid-afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily is brought to the emergency department by her partner. She has had gastroenteritis for 36 hours with vomiting and profuse watery diarrhoea. She has been unable to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose for the last two mornings and has not used her emergency hydrocortisone injection.

On arrival she is drowsy, confused and hypotensive. Blood tests show sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, urea 12.2 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L. Her ambulance BP was 82/54 mmHg. She has been given 1 L normal saline in transit with modest response. There is no fever and she has no meningism.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 88/58 mmHg after 1 L saline (initial 82/54), respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, orientated to person only; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; no focal neurology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg immediately with anti-emetic and observation for the next 2 hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy is not reliable in a vomiting hypotensive patient; parenteral hydrocortisone is required. (Source: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance

options.text: IV fludrocortisone 200 microgram daily as the primary steroid replacement for the crisis today
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid without significant glucocorticoid effect at replacement doses; hydrocortisone provides both at high dose. (Source: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and 200 mg per 24 hours infusion with continued fluid resuscitation and glucose
options.rationale: Australian endocrine guidance for adrenal crisis is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately followed by 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg six-hourly) plus fluid, electrolyte and glucose correction. (Source: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance

options.text: IV dexamethasone 4 mg bolus and reload with oral hydrocortisone when she can tolerate it
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity needed in adrenal crisis with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia; hydrocortisone is preferred. (Source: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance

options.text: IV prednisolone 25 mg bolus and delay definitive replacement until adrenal axis testing has been completed
options.rationale: Diagnostic testing should not delay hydrocortisone treatment in a known primary adrenal insufficiency patient with crisis. (Source: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency in primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency, typically precipitated by illness, missed doses, surgery, trauma or emotional stress. Recognition rests on the combination of shock (relative hypotension, tachycardia), electrolyte disturbance (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia in primary), hypoglycaemia, and often reduced conscious state. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous infusion (or 50 mg six-hourly IV or IM), rapid IV crystalloid to correct volume and sodium deficit, and glucose replacement. At these doses hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect so separate fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. Precipitating illness must be treated concurrently.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours infusion is standard.
Aggressive fluid and glucose correction alongside steroid replacement.
Fludrocortisone not needed acutely at these hydrocortisone doses.
Sick day rules and emergency IM hydrocortisone at home prevent recurrence.
explanation.pearls: In adrenal crisis give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus and 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion with IV fluid and glucose; no separate fludrocortisone needed acutely.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Australia adrenal insufficiency guidance

stem:
A 52-year-old man presents with 4 days of ascending symmetrical lower limb weakness, now involving his hands. He had a diarrhoeal illness 2 weeks ago that resolved spontaneously. On examination he has 3/5 power in both legs, reduced deep tendon reflexes globally, and mild bilateral facial weakness. His forced vital capacity is 1.6 L (predicted 4.5 L), and his single breath count is 12. His swallow is intact and he has no autonomic instability.

A lumbar puncture shows CSF protein 1.2 g/L, WCC 4 cells/microL (<5), glucose 3.8 mmol/L (blood 5.2). Nerve conduction studies were requested and are pending. He is otherwise well with no comorbidities. He has been admitted to the neurology high-dependency bay.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral 3/5 lower limb weakness; upper limb 4/5; areflexia; mild facial diplegia; sensory pinprick reduced distally; intact swallow; no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: FVC 1.6 L (predicted 4.5); single breath count 12; CSF protein 1.2 g/L (<0.45); CSF WCC 4 cells/microL (<5); glucose 3.8 mmol/L (blood 5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunotherapy plan?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 60 mg daily with taper over 8 weeks and no other immunotherapy
options.rationale: Oral corticosteroids are not evidence-based for GBS and delay definitive treatment. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources)

options.text: IV rituximab 1 g single dose targeting B-cell mediated autoantibody production as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Rituximab is not indicated for acute GBS; IVIG or plasma exchange is the standard. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources)

options.text: Observation only with physiotherapy input and no immunomodulatory therapy as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Progressive weakness with FVC below 20 mL/kg requires immunotherapy to shorten hospital stay and reduce ventilation risk. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources)

options.text: IV immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days with respiratory function monitoring and ventilation preparation
options.rationale: IVIG 2 g/kg divided over 5 days is first-line for GBS with clinical features of respiratory compromise or rapidly progressive weakness; plasmapheresis is equally effective. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources; Australian eTG Neurology - GBS)

options.text: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days as first-line to hasten recovery as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not effective in GBS and are not first-line treatment; IVIG or plasma exchange is standard. (Source: RACP Guillain-Barre syndrome resources)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) is an immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy typically triggered by preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Zika, Mycoplasma) 1 to 4 weeks earlier. Diagnosis rests on progressive weakness plus areflexia, supported by albuminocytological dissociation on CSF (raised protein with normal cell count) and nerve conduction studies showing demyelination. Prognostic markers for respiratory failure include rapid progression, bulbar weakness, autonomic instability and FVC below 20 mL/kg (or 1 L in an average adult). Treatment is IVIG 2 g/kg divided over 5 days OR plasma exchange (5 sessions over 2 weeks); the two are equally effective but not combined. Corticosteroids are ineffective and not used.
key_points: IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days is first-line; plasma exchange is equally effective.
Corticosteroids are ineffective in GBS.
FVC below 20 mL/kg or 1 L predicts need for ventilation.
Erasmus GBS Respiratory Insufficiency Score aids risk stratification.
explanation.pearls: In GBS with rapidly progressive weakness and FVC 1.6 L, start IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and admit for respiratory monitoring; steroids do not help.

subtopic_detail: Cardiogenic vs septic shock differentiation with a disconfirming finding
stem: You are the ICU registrar assessing a 68-year-old woman admitted 6 hours ago with fever, dysuria and hypotension after 2 days of urinary sepsis. She initially responded to 30 mL/kg crystalloid and IV gentamicin plus ampicillin. She is now deteriorating despite noradrenaline at 0.4 microgram/kg/min; her BP has fallen to 82/48 mmHg, urine output has dropped to 10 mL/hour and lactate has risen from 3.4 to 5.2 mmol/L. Her ECG shows new T-wave inversion in V4 to V6, JVP is elevated 6 cm above sternal angle, and there are new fine bibasal crackles on auscultation. Bedside echocardiogram shows moderately reduced LV systolic function (EF 30 percent, prior TTE 6 months ago was normal) with no significant valve lesion or pericardial effusion. Troponin is 480 ng/L (<20) rising from 60 ng/L 4 hours ago. Point-of-care ultrasound of the IVC shows a distended 2.4 cm IVC with less than 30 percent respiratory variation.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg on noradrenaline 0.4 microgram/kg/min, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 92 percent on 6 L via mask, temperature 37.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cool clammy peripheries; JVP 6 cm above sternal angle; new fine bibasal crackles; S3 gallop; peripheral oedema absent
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.2 mmol/L (rising from 3.4); troponin 480 ng/L (baseline <20, rising from 60); ECG anterolateral T inversion; TTE EF 30 percent (baseline normal 6 months ago); IVC distended 2.4 cm with reduced variation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her circulatory support?

options.text: Give a further 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and increase noradrenaline to 0.8 microgram/kg/min as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Additional fluid in the presence of raised JVP, crackles and plethoric IVC will worsen pulmonary oedema and cardiac strain. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)

options.text: Add IV vasopressin 0.03 unit/min alone without any inotrope or fluid adjustment with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Vasopressin has a role as second-line vasopressor in septic shock but does not address the cardiogenic component driving the deterioration. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)

options.text: Withdraw the noradrenaline and switch to IV metaraminol 10 mg boluses as needed with routine outpatient follow-up
options.rationale: Bolus vasopressor use is a temporising measure in the ward setting; noradrenaline infusion is preferred in septic and mixed shock. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)

options.text: Give IV furosemide 80 mg alone and continue current haemodynamic support without inotrope as the sole intervention
options.rationale: Diuresis in a patient with cardiogenic shock and a rising lactate risks worsening hypotension; inotropic support must come first. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock)

options.text: Add dobutamine 5 microgram/kg/min IV and stop further fluid resuscitation; arrange urgent cardiology review for possible mechanical support
options.rationale: New troponin rise, ECG changes, reduced EF and IVC plethora indicate superimposed cardiogenic shock; further fluids worsen pulmonary oedema, while inotropes and cardiology input address the LV dysfunction. (Source: Australian eTG: Critical care - Shock; RACP Cardiology guidance)

explanation.summary: Differentiating shock subtypes is essential in the deteriorating ICU patient. Septic shock characteristically features warm peripheries early, low SVR, high or normal cardiac output, and a collapsible IVC after fluid resuscitation. Cardiogenic shock features cool peripheries, high SVR (often reflected clinically in peripheral shutdown), reduced cardiac output, raised JVP, pulmonary crackles, plethoric IVC and evidence of pump failure on echocardiography. The clue in this case is the emergence of ECG ischaemic changes, rising troponin, new LV dysfunction on echo and IVC plethora, in a patient already on high-dose noradrenaline. This suggests demand ischaemia (type 2 MI) or superimposed acute cardiomyopathy driven by sepsis (septic cardiomyopathy or takotsubo).
key_points: Plethoric IVC with pulmonary crackles argues against fluid-responsive septic shock alone.
Rising troponin and new ECG changes suggest superimposed cardiogenic component.
Inotropic support (dobutamine or adrenaline) addresses the pump failure.
Further fluid worsens pulmonary oedema in cardiogenic shock.
explanation.pearls: In septic shock with rising troponin, new LV dysfunction and IVC plethora, switch strategy from further fluid to inotropic support with dobutamine and urgent cardiology input for mechanical support consideration.

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis modified Duke criteria and empirical antibiotic
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 68-year-old woman on the acute medical unit with 3 weeks of malaise, unintentional 3 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats and a low grade fever. She had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 4 years ago for severe calcific aortic stenosis. She has no intravenous drug use history and no recent dental work. She lives in inner Perth.

On examination she is unwell but not septic. There is a soft ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area unchanged from her clinic notes and a new small area of petechiae on her right conjunctiva; no other embolic signs and no splinter haemorrhages. Chest is clear. Abdomen is soft with no tenderness. Two sets of blood cultures taken 12 hours apart both grow Streptococcus sanguinis, and a transthoracic echocardiogram today shows a 6 mm vegetation on the bioprosthetic aortic valve leaflet with mild valvular regurgitation. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Soft ejection systolic murmur aortic area, small right conjunctival petechial patch, no splinter haemorrhages, no splenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Two sets of blood cultures 12 hours apart both positive for Streptococcus sanguinis; transthoracic echocardiogram 6 mm vegetation on bioprosthetic aortic valve with mild regurgitation; CRP 82 mg/L (<10); WCC 10.4 x10^9/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L

lead_in: Which regimen best meets Australian empirical treatment for her prosthetic valve endocarditis while susceptibilities are pending?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily with rifampicin 300 mg twice daily as an outpatient management plan
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires prolonged intravenous therapy; oral is not appropriate for empirical treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours as monotherapy for a total treatment duration of 6 weeks
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve viridans strep endocarditis requires combination therapy with an aminoglycoside and gentamicin for the first 2 weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg per kilogram every 12 hours plus rifampicin 600 mg oral twice daily for 6 weeks
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus rifampicin is used for Staphylococcus aureus prosthetic valve endocarditis with penicillin allergy; not first-line for viridans strep. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg per kilogram every 8 hours for 2 weeks
options.rationale: Viridans streptococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis is treated with 6 weeks of penicillin plus 2 weeks of synergistic gentamicin per Therapeutic Guidelines. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg per kilogram every 8 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin covers staphylococci and is not the drug of choice for viridans streptococcal endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Infective Endocarditis)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is diagnosed by the modified Duke criteria: definite endocarditis requires 2 major, or 1 major and 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. Major criteria are typical organisms in 2 separate blood cultures plus evidence of endocardial involvement on imaging (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation, prosthetic dehiscence). Native valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis is treated with 4 weeks of penicillin or ceftriaxone, or 2 weeks combined with gentamicin. Prosthetic valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis is treated with 6 weeks of penicillin plus 2 weeks of gentamicin; surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation, abscess or prosthetic dehiscence.
key_points: Two positive blood cultures with typical organism plus echo evidence = definite endocarditis.
Prosthetic viridans strep endocarditis: penicillin 6 weeks plus gentamicin 2 weeks.
Native viridans strep endocarditis: penicillin 4 weeks or penicillin plus gentamicin 2 weeks.
Surgical indications include heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation, abscess.
explanation.pearls: Prosthetic valve viridans streptococcal endocarditis in Australia is treated with 6 weeks of intravenous benzylpenicillin plus synergistic gentamicin for the first 2 weeks.

stem:
You are the general medical registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man born in Vietnam who moved to Australia at age 18. He is being worked up in your outpatient clinic for adalimumab therapy for severe Crohn's disease not responding to azathioprine. He is otherwise well and has no cough, weight loss, night sweats or contact with active tuberculosis in the last year. His BCG vaccination scar is visible on his left deltoid from childhood. He has no HIV and is not on other immunosuppressants.

Pre-treatment screening includes a chest radiograph reported as clear with no evidence of prior granulomatous disease. His QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) assay returns positive with TB1 antigen minus nil of 1.6 IU/mL and TB2 antigen minus nil of 1.9 IU/mL (positive cut-off 0.35 IU/mL or higher). Baseline sputum microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF are negative on three morning samples.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, chest clear on auscultation, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph clear; QFT-Plus TB1 1.6 IU/mL and TB2 1.9 IU/mL (positive cut-off 0.35 or higher); sputum microscopy and Xpert MTB/RIF negative x 3; HIV negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step before starting adalimumab?

options.text: Proceed with adalimumab now because BCG history explains a false positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus result
options.rationale: Interferon-gamma release assays are not affected by prior BCG vaccination unlike tuberculin skin testing; a positive QFT-Plus indicates latent tuberculosis infection. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Commence rifampicin plus isoniazid plus pyrazinamide plus ethambutol for 6 months for active pulmonary tuberculosis
options.rationale: There is no evidence of active disease (asymptomatic, clear CXR, negative sputum); full RIPE regimen is not required. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Repeat the QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus assay in 6 months and defer adalimumab until then to observe for indeterminate result
options.rationale: Repeat testing delays biologic therapy without adding information; a clearly positive QFT-Plus with negative active-disease workup is latent tuberculosis requiring treatment. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Perform tuberculin skin test to confirm latent tuberculosis before initiating any treatment given prior BCG vaccination
options.rationale: QFT-Plus is not falsely positive from BCG and the result is already diagnostic of latent tuberculosis; tuberculin skin testing would not add value. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

options.text: Start isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 9 months for latent tuberculosis before adalimumab initiation
options.rationale: Standard LTBI treatment before TNF-alpha inhibitor is 9 months of isoniazid with pyridoxine; 3 months rifampicin/isoniazid is an alternative. (Source: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance)
source_refs: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

explanation.summary: Screening for latent tuberculosis is required before starting biologic therapy or other significant immunosuppression, because reactivation carries high morbidity. Screening involves symptom review, chest radiograph and either tuberculin skin test or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA); IGRAs are preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals as they are not affected by prior vaccination. Positive screening with negative active-disease workup indicates latent tuberculosis. Standard treatment options are 9 months of isoniazid plus pyridoxine, 4 months of rifampicin, or 3-4 months of combined rifampicin plus isoniazid; biologic therapy can begin after at least 4 weeks of LTBI treatment.
key_points: IGRAs are unaffected by BCG vaccination unlike tuberculin skin testing.
Positive IGRA plus negative active-disease workup indicates latent tuberculosis.
Standard LTBI treatment: 9 months isoniazid plus pyridoxine.
Biologic can begin after at least 4 weeks of LTBI treatment.
explanation.pearls: Before TNF-alpha inhibitor start in a BCG-vaccinated patient, a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus with clear CXR is latent TB; treat with 9 months of isoniazid plus pyridoxine.

sources.label: Australian National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guidance

You are the medical registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 74-year-old man is brought in by ambulance with a 24-hour history of confusion, poor oral intake and rigors. He was recently discharged after a 5-day admission for community-acquired pneumonia treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin. His usual medications are ramipril, metformin and rosuvastatin.

On arrival he is sleepy but rousable, with warm peripheries and a productive cough. Chest examination reveals crackles at the right base. Blood cultures have been taken and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g plus gentamicin 5 mg per kilogram have already been given within the first hour. He has received 30 mL per kilogram of intravenous crystalloid over the last 60 minutes. Despite this his blood pressure remains 82/48 mmHg, mean arterial pressure 60 mmHg, with ongoing tachycardia and rising serum lactate from 4.2 to 5.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, MAP 60 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 94 percent on 4 L nasal prong, temperature 39.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, warm peripheries, productive cough, right basal crackles, urine output 20 mL in the last hour
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 5.1 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) rising from 4.2 mmol/L; WCC 21 x10^9/L; CRP 340 mg/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 90 micromol/L); Hb 128 g/L; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence noradrenaline infusion titrated to a target mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg or higher
options.rationale: Persistent hypotension and rising lactate after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid meet septic shock criteria; noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor targeting MAP 65 or above per the Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS guidance. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Give a further 30 mL per kilogram intravenous crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes before commencing vasopressor
options.rationale: Continued aggressive fluid loading after 30 mL/kg with persistent hypotension risks pulmonary oedema; vasopressor is the appropriate escalation. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Add intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg daily as continuous infusion for septic shock without vasopressor
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone in septic shock is used in refractory shock requiring ongoing vasopressor; it is not a first-line replacement for vasopressor. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Order urgent contrast computed tomography of chest to identify pulmonary embolism as alternative diagnosis
options.rationale: The clinical picture is septic shock from likely pneumonia; delaying vasopressor for imaging is inappropriate at this stage of resuscitation. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

options.text: Commence adrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram per kilogram per minute as first-line vasopressor for septic shock
options.rationale: Adrenaline is a second-line agent for septic shock; noradrenaline is first-line based on lower arrhythmogenicity. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis Guidance)

explanation.summary: The sepsis hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate, obtain blood cultures, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate 4 mmol/L or higher, and start vasopressors during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain MAP 65 mmHg or higher. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor, with vasopressin added second-line to reduce noradrenaline dose and adrenaline reserved for refractory shock. Hydrocortisone 200 mg daily is added for shock refractory to fluid and vasopressor. Source control and lactate clearance monitoring guide ongoing management.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if needed.
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor targeting MAP 65 mmHg or higher.
Vasopressin added second-line; adrenaline for refractory shock.
Hydrocortisone added for refractory shock on ongoing vasopressor.
explanation.pearls: In septic shock with persistent hypotension after 30 mL/kg crystalloid, start noradrenaline first-line targeting mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg.

You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man in the emergency department with 24 hours of left leg pain and redness. He has type 2 diabetes on metformin (last HbA1c 8.4 percent). He recalls no obvious skin breach but scraped the shin on a garden edge 3 days ago. The pain has become severe out of proportion to the skin appearance and he is now unable to weight bear.

On examination there is erythema extending from the shin proximally to mid-thigh with tenderness far beyond the erythema margins. The overlying skin has a dusky purple hue in the centre with early bullae. Crepitus is not palpable but there is marked oedema. He is diaphoretic and confused. Bloods show WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 380 mg/L (<10), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), glucose 18 mmol/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (135-175). His LRINEC score is calculated at 9. Plain radiograph of the leg shows no gas in the tissues.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Erythema shin to mid-thigh with tenderness beyond margins; dusky purple hue with early bullae centrally; marked oedema; unable to weight bear
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 380 mg/L (<10); sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145); creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88); glucose 18 mmol/L; Hb 128 g/L (135-175); LRINEC 9; plain radiograph no soft-tissue gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours and reassess clinical progress in the next 24 hours
options.rationale: The clinical picture and LRINEC score of 6 or above are highly suggestive of necrotising fasciitis; standard cellulitis antibiotics alone would miss the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for exploration and debridement with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics
options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis requires urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin); mortality rises with every hour of delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Order urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the leg before deciding on antibiotic or surgical intervention
options.rationale: MRI is sensitive but requesting imaging must not delay surgical exploration in septic patients with a strong clinical picture; exploration is the definitive diagnostic step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Give a therapeutic dose of enoxaparin subcutaneously to cover the possibility of an occlusive vascular event
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is not indicated here and could complicate imminent surgical exploration for necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

options.text: Discharge with oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily and mark the erythema for review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Discharge is unsafe in a septic patient with signs of necrotising infection; inpatient surgical and antibiotic management is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality of around 20-30 percent even with treatment. Discriminators from cellulitis include pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, dusky discolouration, bullae, subcutaneous crepitus (less than 40 percent of cases) and firm woody induration; absence of gas on plain radiograph does not exclude it. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) 6 or above suggests intermediate risk and 8 or above high risk. Management is urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin), with clindamycin included specifically to suppress exotoxin production.
key_points: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, bullae, systemic toxicity suggest necrotising fasciitis.
LRINEC score of 6+ intermediate risk, 8+ high risk.
Absence of tissue gas does not exclude the diagnosis.
Urgent surgical debridement plus piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin, vancomycin.
explanation.pearls: In a septic patient with pain out of proportion, dusky skin and LRINEC 6 or above, arrange urgent surgical debridement with piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin; imaging must not delay theatre.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Necrotising Skin Infections
Australian eTG: Infectious Diseases - Necrotising skin infections
